Lady Benoch's Words and Philosophy

[pagebreak] [pagebreak]

Lady Allena Benoch, former master of the Valenwood Fighter's Guild and head of the Emperor's personal guard in the Imperial City, has been leading a campaign to reacquaint the soldiers of Tamriel with the sword. I met with her on three different occasions for the purposes of this book. The first time was at her suite in the palace, on the balcony overlooking the gardens below. I was early for the interview, which had taken me nearly six months to arrange, but she gently chided me for not being even earlier. "I've had time to put up my defenses now," she said, her bright green eyes smiling. Lady Benoch is a Bosmer, a Wood Elf, and like her ancestors, took to the bow in her early years. She excelled at the sport, and by the age of fourteen, she had joined the hunting party of her tribe as a Jaqspur, a long distance shooter. During the black year of 396, when the Parikh tribe began their rampage through southeastern Valenwood with the aid of powers from the Summurset Isle, Lady Benoch fought the futile battle to keep her tribe's land. "I killed someone for the first time when I was sixteen," she says now. "I don't remember it very well -- he or she was just a blur on the horizon where I aimed my bow. It meant no more to me than shooting animals. I probably killed a hundred people like that during that summer and fall. I didn't really feel like a killer until that wintertide, when I learned what it was like to look into a man's eyes as you spilled his blood. "It was a scout from the Parikh tribe who surprised me while I was on camp watch. We surprised each other, I suppose. I had my bow at my side, and I just panicked, trying to string an arrow when he was half a yard away from me. It was the only thing I knew to do. Of course, he struck first with his blade, and I just fell back in shock." "You always remember the mistakes of your first victim. His mistake was assuming because he had drawn blood and I had fallen, that I was dead. I rushed at him the moment he turned from me towards the sleeping camp of my tribesmen. He was caught off guard, and I wrested his blade away from him." "I don't know how many times I stabbed at him. By the time I stopped, when the next watch came to relieve me, my arms were black and blue with strain, there was not a solid piece of him left. I had literally cut him into pieces. You see, I had no concept of how to fight or how much it took to kill a man." Lady Benoch, aware of this deficiency in her education, began teaching herself swordsmanship at once. "You can't learn how to use a sword in Valenwood," she says. "Which isn't to say Bosmer can't use blades, but we're largely self-taught. As much as it hurt when my tribe found itself homeless, pushed to the north, it did have one good aspect: it afforded me the opportunity to meet Redguards." Studying all manners of weapon wielding under the tutelage of Warday A'kor, Lady Benoch excelled. She became a freelance adventurer, traveling through the wilds of southern Hammerfell and northern Valenwood, protecting caravans and visiting dignitaries from the various dangers indigenous to the population. Unfortunately, before we were able to pursue her story of her early years any further, Lady Benoch was called away on urgent summons from the Emperor. Such is often the case with the Imperial Guard, and in these troubled times, perhaps, more so than in the past. When I tried to contact her for another talk, her servants informed me than their mistress was in Skyrim. Another month passed, and when I visited her suite, I was told she was in High Rock. To her credit, Lady Benoch actually sought me out for our second interview on Sun's Dusk of that year. I was in a tavern in the City called the Blood and Rooster, when I felt her hand on my shoulder. She sat down at the rude table and continued her tale as if it had never been interrupted. She returned to the theme of her days as an adventurer, and told me about the first time she ever felt confident with a sword. "I owned at that time an enchanted daikatana, quite a good one, of daedric metal. It wasn't an original Akaviri, not even of design. I didn't have that kind of money, but it served my primary purpose of delivering as much damage with as little effort on my part as possible. A'kor had taught me how to fence, but when faced with a life or death situation, I always fell back on the old overhand wallop." "A pack of orcs had stolen some gold from a local chieftain in Meditea, and I went looking for them in one of the ubiquitous dungeons that dot the countryside in that region. There were the usual rats and giant spiders, and I was enough of a veteran by then to dispatch them with relative ease. The problem came when I found myself in a pitch black room, and all around me, I heard the grunts of orcs nearing in." "I waved my sword around me, connecting with nothing, hearing their footsteps coming ever nearer. Somehow, I managed to hold back my fear and to remember the simple exercises Master A'kor had taught me. I listened, stepped sideways, swung, twisted, stepped forward, swung a circle, turned around, side-stepped, swung." "My instinct was right. The orcs had gathered in a circle around me, and when I found a light, I saw that they were all dead." "That's when I focused on my study of swordplay. I'm stupid enough to require a near death experience to see the practical purposes, you see." Lady Benoch spent the remainder of the interview, responding in her typically blunt way to the veracity of various myths that surrounded her and her career. It was true that she became the master of the Valenwood Fighter's Guild after winning a duel with the former master, who was a stooge of the Imperial Battlemage, the traitor Jagar Tharn. It was not true that she was the one responsible for the Valenwood Guild's disintegration two years later ("Actually, the membership in the Valenwood chapter was healthy, but in Tamriel overall the mood was not conducive for the continued existence of a nonpartisan organization of freelance warriors.") It was true that she first came to the Emperor's attention when she defended Queen Akorithi of Sentinel from a Breton assassin. It was not true that the assassin was hired by someone in the high court of Daggerfall ("At least," she says wryly, "That has never been proven."). It was also true that she married her former servant Urken after he had been in her service for eleven years ("No one knows how to keep my weaponry honed like he does," she says. "It's a practical business. I either had to give him a raise or marry him."). The only story I asked her that she would neither admit nor refute was the one about Calaxes, the Emperor's bastard. When I brought up the name, she shrugged, professing no knowledge of the affair. I pressed on with the details of the story. Calaxes, though not in line for succession, had been given the Archbishopric of The One: a powerful position in the Imperial City, and indeed over all Tamriel where that religion is honored. Whispering began immediately that Calaxes believed that the Gods were angered with the secular governments of Tamriel and the Emperor specifically. It was even said that Calaxes advocated full-scale rebellion to establish a theocracy over the Empire. It is certainly true, I pressed on, that the Emperor's relationship with Calaxes had become very stormy, and that legislation had been passed to limit the Church's authority. That is, up until the moment when Calaxes disappeared, suddenly, without notice to his closest of friends. Many said that Lady Benoch and the Imperial Guard assassinated the Archbishop Calaxes in the sacristy of his church -- the date usually given was the 29th of Sun's Dusk 3E 498. "Of course," responds Lady Benoch with one of her mysterious grins. "I don't need to tell you that the Imperial Guard's position is as protectors of the throne, not assassins." "But surely, no one is more trusted that the Guard for such a sensitive operation," I say, carefully. Lady Benoch acknowledges that, but merely says that such details of her duties must remain secret as a matter of Imperial security. Unfortunately, her ladyship had to leave early the next morning, as the Emperor had business down south -- of course, I couldn't be told more specifics. She promised to send me word when she returned so we could continue our interview. As it turned out, I had business of my own in the Summurset Isle, compiling a book on the Psijic Order. It was therefore with surprise that I met her ladyship three months later in Firsthold. We managed to get away from our respective duties to complete our third and final interview, on a walk along the Diceto, the great river that passes through the royal parks of the city. Steering away from questions of her recent duties and assignments, which I guessed rightly she was loath to answer, I returned to the subject of swordfighting. "Frandar Hunding," she says. "Lists thirty-eight grips, seven hundred and fifty offensive and eighteen hundred defensive positions, and nearly nine thousand moves essential to sword mastery. The average hack-and-slasher knows one grip, which he uses primarily to keep from dropping his blade. He knows one offensive position, facing his target, and one defensive position, fleeing. Of the multitudinous rhythms and inflections of combat, he knows less than one. "The ways of the warrior were never meant to be the easiest path. The archetype of the idiot fighter is as solidly ingrained as that of the brilliant wizard and the shrewd thief, but it was not always so. The figure of the philosopher swordsman, the blade-wielding artist are creatures of the past, together with the swordsinger of the Redguards, who was said to be able to create and wield a blade with but the power of his mind. The future of the intelligent blade-wielder looks bleak in comparison to the glories of the past." Not wanting to end our interviews on a sour note, I pressed Lady Allena Benoch for advice for young blade-swingers just beginning their careers. "When confronted with a wizard," she says, throwing petals of Kanthleaf into the Diceto. "Close the distance and hit 'im hard."

阿伦娜·贝诺奇夫人，威伦森林的战士公会前任会长兼帝都的皇帝亲卫长，一直在领导一场让泰姆瑞尔士兵们重新熟悉剑这种武器的运动。为了撰写本书，我和她在三个不同场合下会面。第一次安排在她位于宫内的套间中，我们坐在俯瞰下方花园的阳台上。 我花了将近六个月的时间来准备此次访谈，但在我提前抵达时，她却礼貌地温柔责备我没有更早点来。 “现在我已有时间建立我的防线了。”她道，翠绿的眼眸含着笑意。 贝诺奇夫人是波斯莫（木精灵），如其先祖那般，她早年就开始学习使用弓箭。她十分精通箭术，14岁便加入了部落的狩猎队，成为了一名“贾斯普尔”（翻译过来就是长距离弓手）。在396年那黑暗的一年中，得到夏暮岛助力的帕里克部落开始肆虐威伦森林东南部，贝诺奇夫人为保卫部落土地而投身这场毫无意义的战争。 “我第一次杀人时才十六岁，” 她说道， “已经不太记得了--在我引弓瞄准时，他们看起来只是地平线上一个模糊的身影。对我而言，与杀死一头野兽没什么区别。那年夏秋我杀了大概一百人。直到那年冬天，当我把敌人杀得鲜血横飞，看着他的眼睛时，我才真正感觉自己是个杀手了。” “正当我在营地警戒时，帕里克部落的一个斥候突然出现在我的视野里，把我吓了一跳。我们应该把彼此都吓着了吧。我的弓就放在我身侧，但我早已陷入慌乱，打算在他离我只有半码远的时候射箭。当时我心里只想到了这一个办法。当然了，那么近的情况下自然是他先发制人以刀刺中了我。我被吓倒在地。” “你总会对杀掉的第一个人所犯的错误记忆犹新。而他犯下的错误便是在看到我失血倒下之后就当我已经死了。待他转向我们部族士兵休息的营地时，我就暴起扑向他。猝不及防之下，他的剑就被我夺下了。” “已经不记得我到底捅了他多少刀，直到我的战友前来换防才停止。我的双臂因用力过度的扭伤而青紫片片，他的尸块无一可辨。我真是把他剁得不能再碎了。你看，那时的我丝毫不知道怎么打斗，也不知道杀一个人要花多少气力。” 贝诺奇夫人意识到自身在这方面训练的不足，当即开始自修剑术。 “你在威伦森林学不到什么剑术，”她说， “我不是说波斯莫不会用剑，主要是因为我们当中绝大多数人都是自学成才。我的部落在这期间无家可归，被迫北上逃难，我满心悲痛。然而也不是没有好处，我有机会遇到红卫人了。 贝诺奇夫人拜入瓦尔代·阿’柯尔门下，学习各种武器的使用方法，表现非凡。她由此成了自由探险家。穿行往来于落锤省南部和威伦森林北部间的荒野，护卫商队和来访政要免遭当地民众所面临的各种危险。 不幸的是，我们还没来得及更深入探讨她早年故事的细节，贝诺奇夫人就被皇帝紧急召见离去了。这对帝国卫队而言是家常便饭，尤其在这动荡时期，自然是更胜以往。在我试着和她联络再访谈一次时，她的仆人们却告知我他们的女主人已前往天际。又过一月，我再度造访，又被告知其已身在高岩。 值得称道的是，贝诺奇夫人实际上在那年日暮月找我进行了我们的第二次访谈。那时我在城中一所名为“鲜血与雄鸡”的客栈，突然感到她的手搭在我肩上。她随即在粗糙的酒桌一侧坐下，继续讲述她的故事，好像从没有人打断过我们的交谈。 她又讲述起昔日冒险家的话题，然后对我述说起她第一次对用剑感到自信的那件往事。 “当年我用的是一柄非常出色的、迪德拉金属锻造的附魔大太刀。它并非原产于阿卡维尔，甚至连设计上也不尽相同。我那时没那么多钱。但这把刀足以满足我的主要需求了，即以尽可能少的力道造成尽可能多的伤害。阿’柯尔曾教授我如何击剑，可在面临生死一念间之时，我总会回到老一套的乱砍猛攻。” “一伙兽人盗去了麦蒂提当地酋长的钱，我一路追踪他们到当地郊区数不胜数的地牢之一。那里市场有恶鼠和巨蛛出没，而那时的我经验已经很丰富了，打发它们还很轻松。问题来了，当我身处一个漆黑房间时，我听到周围兽人的咕哝声越来越近。” “我不断挥剑，却全都扑空，只能听见他们的脚步声越发逼近。不知怎的，我竟成功克制恐惧，并回忆起阿’柯尔大师教授的简单剑技。我聆听，侧步，舞剑，回旋身，返身前扑，剑舞一圈，回身收势，侧步，舞剑。” “我直觉无误。兽人们正聚集在我周围。待我寻得光源后，只见他们尽数身亡伏地。” “正是那时，我才开始真正专心于剑术学习。我真傻，没经历一次濒死体验，都不能理解剑术的意义。” 贝诺奇夫人在余下的访谈时间中一直保有她惯有的直爽谈吐回答了围绕她及她事业生涯中种种传奇的真实性。例如，她确实是在决斗中杀死了帝国战斗法师贾伽·萨恩扶植的傀儡才成为了威伦森林战士公会大师。但她不是两年后威伦森林公会解散的罪魁祸首（“实话说吧，威伦森林分会的成员发展健康，但泰姆瑞尔整体秩序不利于自由战士组成的无立场组织继续存在。”）。的确，她第一次引起皇帝注意，是她从布莱顿刺客手下保全了哨卫女王阿珂丽蒂。但至于刺客雇主是匕落宫廷高层中人就纯属虚构（“最起码，”她苦笑着说，“这一点从未被证明。”）。同样的事实是，她与为她劳作11年的前仆人乌尔肯成婚（“没人能像他那么清楚如何为我研磨武器，”她说， “这是一笔很现实的生意。我要么就得给他加薪，要么就和他结婚。”）。 我问及她的所有故事中，她仅对一个问题持模棱两可态度，那便是关于皇帝私生子卡拉克斯的事。我提及此名时，她耸耸肩，声称对此毫不知晓。我继续述说着这故事的相关细节。卡拉克斯虽没有继承权，却就任了至尊神殿大主教一职，在帝都中举足轻重，因为这个信仰体系在整个泰姆瑞尔都备受崇敬。随即就开始有卡拉克斯认为“众神对泰姆瑞尔的世俗政权，尤其是皇帝的所作所为感到愤怒”这类谣言。甚至有言称卡拉克斯谋求发起全境叛乱，建立一个神权政体。 我接着说，皇帝和卡拉克斯的关系变得非常紧张，而且通过立法来限制教会权力。这段时间中，卡拉克斯被发现骤然人间蒸发，连他最贴心的挚友都未注意到他的行程。人道是贝诺奇夫人领御前亲卫在他的神殿圣器室内刺杀了卡拉克斯，通常的说法是第三纪元498年日暮月29日。 “当然，”贝诺奇夫人神秘地莞尔答道，“不用我说你也知道，帝国卫队的职责是保护皇帝，而非去当刺客。” 我小心地选择措辞：“但有一点确凿无疑：没有谁能像你们亲卫这么受信任而能去执行这种敏感行动了。” 贝诺奇夫人承认这点，但只是说关于她的职务细节必须保密，毕竟关乎帝国安全问题。遗憾的是，她明早就要启程离开，跟随皇帝到南部公干——我自然不能得知更多细节了。她承诺在她归来后会致函予我，另约时间继续面谈。 此间事后，为了撰写一本关于赛伊克教团的书籍，我出差往夏暮岛办事。三月后，我在首堡与夫人再度聚首，真让我深感惊讶。我们各自从事务中脱身来完成这第三次也是最末一次的访谈，并约在穿过城中王家花园的迪瑟托河河畔散步。 关于她近来工作和事务的那些敏感问题，我猜她是并不想回答的。我就避开这些，回到最初谈到的剑术问题。 她说：“弗兰达·亨丁列出了握剑38手势，750进攻姿态，1800防御姿态，及近9000种掌握剑术所必须的动作。只晓砍杀的平常人，仅知一种手势，就是保证剑不会掉下来；他仅知一种进攻姿态，就是直面对手；也仅知一种防守姿势，那就是逃跑。对于战斗中的诸多节奏与变化，则是一无所知。” “战士之道没有捷径可走。战士愚蠢好斗的刻板印象就如巫师的聪慧、盗贼的精明一样根深蒂固，然而并不总是如此。对于过去红卫人的剑歌者来说，他们就是一群剑客哲人，把挥剑变成了一种艺术，据说他们可以凭意念创造并挥舞刀剑。与过去的辉煌相比，智慧剑客的未来显得黯淡无光。” 我还不打算用陈词滥调结束我们的采访。于是请阿伦娜·贝诺奇夫人给踏入剑道生涯的年轻剑舞者们一些建议。 “如果碰上巫师，”她说着，将一大把坎斯叶的花瓣撒入迪瑟托河，“速逼近，奋力斩。”

n a minor but respectable plaza in the Imperial City sat, or perhaps lounged, Lord Vanech's Building Commission. It was an unimaginative, austere building not noted so much for its aesthetic or architectural design as for its prodigious length. If any critics wondered why such an unornamented, extended erection held such fascination for Lord Vanech, they kept it to themselves. In the 398th year of the 3rd Era, Decumus Scotti was a senior clerk at the Commission. It had been a few months since the shy, middle-aged man had brought Lord Vanech the most lucrative of all contracts, granting the Commission the exclusive right to rebuild the roads of Valenwood which had been destroyed in the Five Year War. For this, he had become the darling of the managers and the clerks, spending his days recounting his adventures, more or less faithfully... although he did omit the ending of the tale, since many of them had partaken in the celebratory Unthrappa roast provided by the Silenstri. Informing one's listeners that they've gorged on human flesh improves very few stories of any good taste. Scotti was neither particularly ambitious nor hard-working, so he did not mind that Lord Vanech had not given him anything to actually do. Whenever the squat little gnomish man would happen upon Decumus Scotti in the offices, Lord Vanech would always say, "You're a credit to the Commission. Keep up the good work." In the beginning, Scotti had worried that he was supposed to be doing something, but as the months went on, he merely replied, "Thank you. I will." There was, on the other hand, the future to consider. He was not a young man, and though he was receiving a respectable salary for someone not doing actual work, Scotti considered that soon he might have to retire and not get paid for not doing work. It would be nice, he decided, if Lord Vanech, out of gratitude for the millions of gold the Valenwood contract was generating, might deign to make Scotti a partner. Or at least give him a small percentage of the bounty. Decumus Scotti was no good at asking for things like that, which was one of the reasons why, previous to his signal successes in Valenwood as a senior clerk for Lord Atrius, he was a lousy agent. He had just about made up his mind to say something to Lord Vanech, when his lordship unexpectedly pushed things along. "You're a credit to the Commission," the waddling little thing said, and then paused. "Do you have a moment free on your schedule?" Scotti nodded eagerly, and followed his lordship to his hideously decorated and very enviable hectare of office space. "Zenithar blesses us for your presence at the Commission," the little fellow squeaked grandly. "I don't know whether you know this, but we were having a bad time before you came along. We had impressive projects, for certain, but they were not successful. In Black Marsh, for example, for years we've been trying to improve the roads and other routes of travel for commerce. I put my best man, Flesus Tijjo, on it, but every year, despite staggering investments of time and money, the trade along those routes only gets slower and slower. Now, we have your very clean, very, very profitable Valenwood contract to boost the Commission's profits. I think it's time you were rewarded." Scotti grinned a grin of great modesty and subtle avarice. "I want you to take over the Black Marsh account from Flesus Tijjo." Scotti shook as if awaking from a pleasant dream to hideous reality, "My Lord, I - I couldn't -" "Nonsense," chirped Lord Vanech. "Don't worry about Tijjo. He will be happy to retire on the money I give him, particularly as soul-wrenchingly difficult as this Black Marsh business has been. Just your sort of a challenge, my dear Decumus." Scotti couldn't utter a sound, though his mouth feebly formed the word "No" as Lord Vanech brought out the box of documentation on Black Marsh. "You're a fast reader," Lord Vanech guessed. "You can read it all en route." "En route to ..." "Black Marsh, of course," the tiny fellow giggled. "You are a funny chap. Where else would you go to learn about the work that's being done, and how to improve it?" The next morning, the stack of documentation hardly touched, Decumus Scotti began the journey south-east to Black Marsh. Lord Vanech had hired an able-bodied guard, a rather taciturn Redguard named Mailic, to protect his best agent. They rode south along the Niben, and then south-east along the Silverfish, continuing on into the wilds of Cyrodiil, where the river tributaries had no names and the very vegetation seemed to come from another world than the nice, civilized gardens of the northern Imperial Province. Scotti's horse was tied to Mailic's, so the clerk was able to read. It made it difficult to pay attention to the path they were taking, but Scotti knew he needed at least a cursory familiarity with the Commission's business dealings in Black Marsh. It was a huge box of paperwork going back forty years, when the Commission had first been given several million in gold by a wealthy trader, Lord Xellicles Pinos-Revina, to improve the condition of the road from Gideon to Cyrodiil. At that time, it took three weeks, a preposterously long time, for the rice and root he was importing to arrive, half-rotten, in the Imperial Province. Pinos-Revina was long dead, but many other investors over the decades, including Pelagius IV himself, had hired the Commission to build roads, drain swamps, construct bridges, devise anti-smuggling systems, hire mercenaries, and, in short, do everything that the greatest Empire in history knew would work to aid trade with Black Marsh. According to the latest figures, the result of this was that it took two and a half months for goods, now thoroughly rotten, to arrive. Scotti found that when he looked up after concentrating on what he was reading, the landscape had always changed. Always dramatically. Always for the worse. "This is Blackwood, sir," said Mailic to Scotti's unspoken question. It was dark and woodsy, so Decumus Scotti thought that a very appropriate name. The question he longed to ask, which in due course he did ask, was, "What's that terrible smell?" "Slough Point, sir," Mailic replied as they turned the next bend, where the umbrageous tunnel of tangled tree and vine opened to a clearing. There squatted a cluster of formal buildings in the dreary Imperial design favored by Lord Vanech's Commission and every Emperor since Tiber, together with a stench so eye-blindingly, stomach-wrenchingly awful that Scotti wondered, suddenly, if it were deadly poisonous. The swarms of blood-colored, sand-grain-sized insects obscuring the air did not improve the view. Scotti and Mailic batted at the buzzing clouds as they rode their horses towards the largest of the buildings, which on approach revealed itself to be perched at the edge of a thick, black river. From its size and serious aspect, Scotti guessed it to be the census and excise office for the wide, white bridge that stretched across the burbling dark water to the reeds on the other side. It was a very nice, bright, sturdy-looking bridge, built, Scotti knew, by his Commission. A poxy, irritable official opened the door quickly on Scotti's first knock. "Come in, come in, quickly! Don't let the fleshflies in!" "Fleshflies?" Decumus Scotti trembled. "You mean, they eat human flesh?" "If you're fool enough to stand around and let them," the soldier said, rolling his eyes. He had half an ear, and Scotti, looking around at the other soldiers in the fort noted that they all were well-chewed. One of them had no nose at all to speak of. "Now, what's your business?" Scotti told them, and added that if they stood outside the fortress instead of inside, they might catch more smugglers. "You better be more concerned with getting across that bridge," the soldier sneered. "Tide's coming up, and if you don't get a move on, you won't get to Black Marsh for four days." That was absurd. A bridge swamped by a rising tide on a river? Only the look in the soldier's eyes told Scotti he wasn't joking. Upon stepping out of the fort, he saw that the horses, evidently tired of being tortured by the fleshflies, had ripped free of their restraints and were bounding off into the woods. The oily water of the river was already lapping on the planks, oozing between the crevices. Scotti reflected that perhaps he would be more than willing to endure a wait of four days before going to Black Marsh, but Mailic was already running across. Scotti followed him, wheezing. He was not in excellent shape, and never had been. The box of Commission materials was heavy. Halfway across, he paused to catch his breath, and then discovered he could not move. His feet were stuck. The black mud that ran through the river was a thick gluey paste, and having washed over the plank Scotti was on, it held his feet fast. Panic seized him. Scotti looked up from his trap and saw Mailic leaping from plank to plank ahead of him, closing fast on the reeds on the other side. "Help!" Scotti cried. "I'm stuck!" Mailic did not even turn around, but kept jumping. "I know, sir. You need to lose weight." Decumus Scotti knew he was a few pounds over, and had meant to start eating less and exercising more, but embarking on a diet hardly seemed to promise timely aid in his current predicament. No diet on Nirn would have helped him just then. However, on reflection, Scotti realized that the Redguard intended that he drop the box of documents, for Mailic was no longer carrying any of the essential supplies he had had with him previously. With a sigh, Scotti threw the box of Commission notes into the glop, and felt the plank under him rise a quarter of an inch, just enough to free him from the mud's clutches. With an agility born of extreme fear, Scotti began leaping after Mailic, dropping onto every third plank, and springing up before the river gripped him. In forty-six leaps, Decumus Scotti crashed through the reeds onto the solid ground behind Mailic, and found himself in Black Marsh. He could hear behind him a slurping sound as the bridge, and his container of important and official records of Commission affairs, was consumed by the rising flood of dark filth, never to be seen again.

帝都一片占地不大但景致宜人的广场上坐落着，或者说松松散散地立着瓦内奇大人的建筑委员会。该建筑毫无创意又毫不起眼，比起美学或建筑设计，它那建造长度更为惹人注目。就算有任何批评家对瓦内奇大人如此钟情于又朴素又长长的建筑的原因感到好奇，他们也不会把这种心理展现出来。 在第三纪元398年，戴奎莫斯·斯科提是该委员会的高级职员。 自打这位内向的中年男子给瓦内奇大人带来最为利益可观的合同（这授予了委员会重建威伦森林在五年战争里损毁道路的专属权）已经过去几个月了。为此，他成为了经理和职员之间的宠儿，许多天以来都在随心所欲地复述他那冒险……不过他确实对故事的结尾避而不谈，因为他们很多人都出席了那场由希伦斯特里提供昂斯拉帕的宴会。告知听众他们吃了人肉，对故事而言可有伤大雅。 斯科提没什么太大的志向，也不怎么刻苦努力，因此他并不是很在意瓦内奇大人让他当了个闲差。 每次这位侏儒般的矮胖小个男人在办公室碰见戴奎莫斯·斯科提时，瓦内奇大人都会说：“你可是委员会的功臣啊。好好工作吧。” 刚开始，斯科提还担心他得干些什么，不过几个月过去了，他只是回答：“谢谢。我会的。” 另一方面，也得考虑考虑将来。他年纪大了，尽管他的工资对于一个闲差而言非常可观，但斯科提觉得他很快就可能会退休，会因为不工作而领不到薪水。他觉得，如果瓦内奇大人出于对威伦森林合同所产生的数以百计金钱的感激，而让斯科提当一位合作伙伴的话，那可真是太棒了。或者至少给他一小笔奖金。 戴奎莫斯·斯科提并不善于提出这样的要求，这也就是他原来作为阿特里乌斯大人的高级职员在威伦森林取得巨大成功前，干得很差劲的原因之一了。就当他下定决心跟瓦内奇大人说点什么时，他家老板出乎意料地把话题岔开了。 “你可是委员会的功臣。”那摇摇晃晃的矮东西说，然后询问道，“你有空吗？” 斯科提热切地点点头，跟着他家老板来到他那间在装潢上品味可怕，面积上又十分引人艳羡的办公室。 “真是托泽尼萨尔的福，能让你进我们委员会，”这小个子装模作样地吱吱，“我不了解你是否清楚此事，不过在你来之前我们的日子可不好过。我们是有显赫的项目，那是当然的，不过我们并不成功。比方说，在黑沼泽，我们已经耗费了数年时间尝试着去改善道路以及其他贸易路线的状况。我派了最好的员工，弗利萨斯·提乔，负责这事，然而尽管投入了惊人的时间和金钱，这些路线上的贸易却逐年减慢。现在，我们有了你那非常正当还非常非常有赚头的威伦森林合同来提高委员会的利润。我想是时候奖励奖励你了。” 斯科提微微一笑，表现出了极大的谦卑以及适度的渴望。 “我想让你接管弗利萨斯·提乔在黑沼泽的业务。” 斯科提好似从美梦跌入丑恶的现实中一样打着颤，“大人，我——我不能——” “没事，”瓦内奇叽叽喳喳道，“别替提乔操心啦。他会很开心地拿着我给他的钱退休，尤其是面对像这桩黑沼泽业务一样让人脑壳炸开的事。亲爱的戴奎莫斯，这事正合适给你挑战挑战。” 尽管当瓦内奇大人拿出那装有黑沼泽文件的箱子时，斯科提的嘴巴虚弱地摆出了“不”的形状，但他却一个字都吐不出来。 “你阅读速度很快，” 瓦内奇大人猜测道，“你能在路上把它读了。” “路上……” “当然是黑沼泽了。”小矮子咯咯笑道，“你这家伙可真有意思。你还能到哪里去了解正在进行的工作，去了解如何改进它呢？” 第二天早晨，戴奎莫斯·斯科提向东南方踏上了去往黑沼泽的旅程，而那堆文件几乎碰也没碰。瓦内奇大人雇了一位体力健硕的保镖保护他最棒的职员，是个叫梅耶里克的沉默寡言的红卫人。他们沿着尼本河向南前进，随后沿着银鱼河转向东南方向，一直走进希罗帝尔的荒野，在那里的支流没有名字，那些植被比起帝国省北部那美丽、文明的花园来，更像是来自异界。 斯科提把马匹跟梅耶里克的拴在一起，以便能够阅读文件。这让他很难去留意他们所走过的路，不过斯科提知道他至少得大致熟悉熟悉委员会在黑沼泽的业务往来。 这是一个装有过去四十年来文件的硕大箱子，那时一个富有的商人，希利克利斯·皮诺斯-雷维纳大人，第一次就给了协会大量金币来改善吉迪昂到希罗帝尔道路的状况。那时，他进口的水稻和根茎要耗费三周的时间才能抵达帝都，而且有一半还烂了，这时间可是太长了。皮诺斯-雷维纳早就去世了，不过过去几十年来许多其他的投资者，包括佩拉吉斯四世本人，都付钱给委员会去修建道路，抽干沼泽，修建桥梁，设计反走私系统，雇佣佣兵，总之是做了这史上最伟大的帝国所能想到的一切来扶持与黑沼泽的贸易。可几番努力下，根据最新的数据，货物要花两个半月的时间才能抵达，而且全都烂掉了。 斯科提发现当他在专心阅读后猛一抬头时，周围的景致总是在变化。变化总是特别剧烈，也总是变得更加险恶。 “这就是黑森林了，先生。” 梅耶里克回答了斯科提心中的疑问。郁郁葱葱，遮天蔽日的森林让戴奎莫斯·斯科提觉得这名字恰如其分。 他一直想问一个问题，后来找了个时机问了出来，那就是：“这难闻的味道是什么啊？” “这里是‘腐沼角’，先生。” 梅耶里克在下一个路口转弯时答道，此地的树木和藤蔓缠绕在一起形成一条隧道，通往一处空地。那里排布着一群相当正式的建筑，那是瓦内奇委员会和自泰伯以来的每位皇帝都十分喜欢却又沉闷无趣的帝国风格，同时还伴随着一股令人头晕目眩、揪心作呕的恶臭，以至于让斯科提怀疑，是不是什么毒药。成群沙粒大小的血色昆虫遮蔽了空气，使得视野不佳。 斯科提和梅耶里克边与嗡嗡作响的云团战斗边直奔最大的建筑群，靠近时才发现它坐落在一条流着黑色粘稠河水的河流边。从它的规模以及肃穆的外观看，斯科提猜测那是座人口及税务办公室，因为有座宽阔的白桥横跨过波光粼粼的黑水。那是座非常漂亮、恢弘、坚固的桥梁，斯科提知道那是他们委员会负责建造的。 一位脸上生痘又脾气暴躁的军官在斯科提敲第一下门时就赶紧开了门。“进门，进门，赶紧的。别让肉蝇进来！” “肉蝇？”戴奎莫斯·斯科提打着颤，“你是说，它们吃人肉？” “如果你蠢到坐着不动让它们吃的话，”士兵转转眼珠说道。他有半只耳朵，斯科提看看周围堡垒里其他的士兵，他们身上都有被咬过的痕迹。其中一位没有鼻子的说道：“好了，你有什么公干？” 斯科提告诉了他们，还补充说如果他们站在堡垒外面而非内部，他们就能抓住更多的走私犯了。 “你最好先想想怎么过桥。”士兵讥笑道，“要涨潮了，如果你不前进的话，你四天都到不了黑沼泽。” 荒谬。河上的桥梁竟会被涨起的潮汐淹没？只有士兵的眼神告诉斯科提他并非在开玩笑。 一走出堡垒，他就看到那些马显然是受够了肉蝇的折磨，它们挣脱了缰绳，跳进了树林里。油乎乎的河水已经拍打着木板，从缝隙间渗出来。斯科提思忖，他宁可再等四天再前往黑沼泽，然而梅耶里克已经过去了。 斯科提气喘吁吁跟上他。他身体状况从来就没好过。装着委员会材料的箱子很是沉重。走到一半，他停下来喘口气，然后发现他动不了了。他的脚被卡住了。 河水中流淌的黑泥根本就是粘稠的浆糊，它漫上斯科提所在的木板，很快吸住了他的双脚。他惊慌失措。斯科提从陷阱里抬起头来，看见梅耶里克在他面前从一块木板跳到另一块木板，很快就要接近对岸了。 “救救我！”斯科提大喊，“我被卡住了！” 梅耶里克甚至没有转头，继续跳着。“我知道，先生。你得减肥了。” 戴奎莫斯·斯科提知道他有点超重，而他已经打算开始节食，多做运动了，然而在目前的困境中，节食显然是来不及了。全奈恩都没有什么饮食计划帮他脱困。不过，经过思考，斯科提明白了那红卫是想让他丢掉装文件的箱子，因为梅耶里克不再带着他以前携带的必须品了。 斯科提叹了口气，将装有委员会备忘录的箱子扔进了泥潭中，随即发觉他脚下的木板上升了四分之一寸，刚刚能把他从泥潭中解放出来。由于极度的恐惧，斯科提开始敏捷地跟着梅耶里克跳跃着，每隔三块木板就落地一次，然后在河水吞没他之前又蹦起身来。 经过四十六次跳跃后，戴奎莫斯·斯科提穿过芦苇落到梅耶里克身后坚实的地面上，发觉自己已经置身于黑沼泽。他听到身后传来咕噜咕噜的声音，上涨的黑色污物吞没了桥梁以及他的行李还有委员会事务官方记录，这些东西再也不见了。

Eslaf Erol was the last of the litter of five born to the Queen of the prosperous Nordic kingdom of Erolgard, Lahpyrcopa, and her husband, the King of Erolgard, Ytluaf. During pregnancy, the Queen had been more than twice as wide as she was tall, and the act of delivery took three months and six days after it had begun. It is perhaps understandable that the Lahpyrcopa elected, upon expelling Eslaf to frown, say, 'Good riddance,' and die. Like many Nords, Ytluaf did not care very much for his wife and less for his children. His subjects were puzzled, therefore, when he announced that he would follow the ancient tradition of his people of Atmora of following his beloved spouse to the grave. They had not thought they were particularly in love, nor were they aware that such a tradition existed. Still, the simple people were grateful, for the little royal drama alleviated their boredom, which was and is a common problem in the more obscure parts of northern Skyrim, particularly in wintertide. He gathered his household staff and his five fat, bawling little heirs in front of him, and divided his estate. To his son Ynohp, he gave his title; to his son Laernu, he gave his land; to his son Suoibud, he gave his fortune; to his daughter Laicifitra, he gave his army. Ytluaf's advisors had suggested he keep the inheritance together for the good of the kingdom, but Ytluaf did not particularly care for his advisors, or the kingdom, for that matter. Upon making his announcement, he drew his dagger across his throat. One of the nurses, who was rather shy, finally decided to speak as the King's life ebbed away. 'Your highness, you forgot your fifth child, little Eslaf.' Good Ytluaf groaned. It is somewhat hard to concentrate with blood gushing from one's throat, after all. The King tried in vain to think of something to bequeath, but there was nothing left. Finally he sputtered, irritably, 'Eslaf should have taken something then' and died. That a babe but a few days old was expected to demand his rightful inheritance was arguably unfair. But so Eslaf Erol was given his birthright with his father's dying breath. He would have nothing, but what he had taken. Since no one else would have him, the shy nurse, whose name was Drusba, took the baby home. It was a decrepit little shack, and over the years that followed, it became more and more decrepit. Unable to find work, Drusba sold all of her furnishings to buy food for little Eslaf. By the time he was old enough to walk and talk, she had sold the walls and the roof as well, so they had nothing but a floor to call home. And if you've ever been to Skyrim, you can appreciate that that is scarcely sufficient. Drusba did not tell Eslaf the story of his birth, or that his brothers and sister were leading quite nice lives with their inheritances, for, as we have said, she was rather shy, and found it difficult to broach the subject. She was so painfully shy, in fact, that whenever he asked any questions about where he came from, Drusba would run away. That was more or less her answer to everything, to flee. In order to communicate with her at all, Eslaf learned how to run almost as soon as he could walk. He couldn't keep up with his adopted mother at first, but in time he learned to go toe-heel toe-heel if he anticipated a short but fast sprint, and heel-toe heel-toe if it seemed Drusba was headed for a long distance marathon flight. He never did get all the answers he needed from her, but Eslaf did learn how to run. The kingdom of Erolgard had, in the years that Eslaf was growing, become quite a grim place. King Ynohp did not have a treasury, for Suoibud had been given that; he did not have any property for income, for Laernu had been given that; he did not have an army to protect the people, for Laicifitra had been given that. Futhermore, as he was but a child, all decisions in the kingdom went through Ynohp's rather corrupt council. It had become a bureaucratic exploitative land of high taxes, rampant crime, and regular incursions from neighboring kingdoms. Not a particular unusual situation for a kingdom of Tamriel, but an unpleasant one nonetheless. The time finally came when the taxcollector arrived to Drusba's hovel, such as it was, to collect the only thing he could - the floor. Rather than protest, the poor shy maid ran away, and Eslaf never saw her again. Without a home or a mother, Eslaf did not know what to do. He had grown accustomed to the cold open air in Drusba's shack, but he was hungry. 'May I have a piece of meat?' he asked the butcher down the street. 'I'm very hungry.' The man had known the boy for years, often spoke to his wife about how sorry he felt for him, growing up in a home with no ceilings or walls. He smiled at Eslaf and said, 'Go away, or I'll hit you.' Eslaf hurriedly left the butcher and went to a nearby tavern. The tavernkeeper had been a former valet in the king's court and knew that the boy was by right a prince. Many times, he had seen the poor ragged lad in the streets, and sighed at the way fate had treated him. 'May I have something to eat?' Eslaf asked this tavernkeeper. 'I'm very hungry.' 'You're lucky I don't cook you up and eat you,' replied the tavernkeeper. Eslaf hurriedly left the tavern. For the rest of the day, the boy approached the good citizens of Erolgard, begging for food. One person had thrown something at him, but it turned out to be an inedible rock. As night fell, a raggedy man came up to Eslaf and, without saying a word, handed him a piece of fruit and a piece of dried meat. The lad took it, wide-eyed, and as he devoured it, he thanked the man very sweetly. 'If I see you begging on the streets tomorrow,' the man growled. 'I'll kill you myself. There are only so many beggars we of the guild allow in any one town, and you make it one too many. You're ruining business.' It was a good thing Eslaf Erol knew how to run. He ran all night. Eslaf Erol's story is continued in the book 'Thief.'

伊斯拉夫·埃罗尔，是繁荣一时的诺德王国埃罗尔嘉德的王后，拉皮尔科帕和她的丈夫伊特卢阿夫王的五胞胎中的老幺。怀孕期间、王后的体宽是身高的两倍，分娩足足持续了三个月零六天。这就能理解为什么拉皮尔科帕把伊斯拉夫生下后紧蹙着眉头说：“算是摆脱了，”然后就此逝世了。 和多数诺德人一样，伊特卢阿夫并不关心自己的妻子，遑论孩子们了。所以当他宣称要遵从阿特莫拉的古老传统给亲爱的夫人殉葬时，他的臣民大感疑惑。他们哪能想到二人相爱如此之深，也没意识到还有这么个传统。不过单纯的人们还是很感谢能有这小小的王室闹剧来缓解他们生活的无聊。无聊在这样一个天际北境的无名地区一度是个普遍问题，尤其是在大冬天。 王召集起他的家人和他那五个胖嘟嘟、大哭大闹的小继承人，开始分家产。王衔给了儿子伊诺普，土地给了儿子拉尔努，国库给了儿子索伊巴德，军队给了女儿莱西菲特拉。伊特卢阿夫的顾问们建议他为了王国的利益着想将遗产合在一处，但伊特卢阿夫并不怎么在乎他的顾问或是王国。他宣布完就拿匕首捅向了喉咙。 王的生命消逝之际，一位非常腼腆的小护士终于决定开口了：“陛下，您忘了您的第五个孩子，小伊斯拉夫。” 伟大的伊特卢阿夫呻吟着。毕竟要在喉咙正往外头喷血时集中精力真是强人所难。国王徒劳地想要遗赠点什么，但这会已经没东西剩下了。 最后他满心暴躁，急促而语无伦次地说：“伊斯拉夫得拿到点啥。”然后就崩殂了。 希望一个才几天大的婴儿会索要他的合法继承权实在很不公平。于是伊斯拉夫·埃罗尔随父亲的临终一息被赋予了他与生俱来的权利。他什么都得不到，除了他已经得到的。 因为没人肯收养他，于是那名叫德鲁丝芭的腼腆小护士将婴儿抱回家。那是一间破旧的棚屋，而且自那之后几年里一年比一年破旧。因为找不到工作，德鲁丝芭卖掉她的全副家当来喂小伊斯拉夫。待他长到能走路和说话时，她已经将四壁和房顶也卖了个干净。于是他们仅剩一面地板可以称为家了。如果你曾经来过天际，你就会明白这日子根本没法过。 德鲁丝芭没告诉伊斯拉夫他的离奇身世，也没说他的兄姐们拿着遗产而逍遥快活。因为正如我所说，她腼腆得紧，难以启齿道出个中原委。事实上她腼腆到每当他问起他自哪里来的问题，德鲁丝芭都会跑开。那或多或少就是她对待一切事情的方式了，逃避。 为了能和她沟通，伊斯拉夫几乎在刚会走时就学会了跑。起初，他自然跟不上他养母的步子，但随着时间推移，他学会了：如果他想急奔、就先脚趾着地再脚跟着地跑;如果德鲁丝芭看起来要来段大长跑，他就会脚跟着地再脚趾着地地跑。他从未自她那得到他所需要的所有答案，但伊斯拉夫确实学会了怎么跑。 埃罗尔嘉德王国在伊斯拉夫成长的年月里变成了一个很吓人的地方。伊诺普王没国库，因为索伊巴德拿走了;他没有能征税的地产，因为拉尔努拿走了;他没有军队保护百姓，因为莱西菲特拉拿走了。另外，由于他还是个孩子，王国内所有的决策都要经过伊诺普那极度腐败的议会拍板。这里变成了充斥高额税赋、猖獗犯罪和官僚剥削的地方，还频繁遭邻国入侵。在泰姆瑞尔，这样一个王国并不出奇，但确实令人感到不快。 终于，税务官来到德鲁丝芭那不宜居的小木屋，来收他能收走的唯一东西——地板。可怜腼腆的女仆选择逃跑而非反抗，伊斯拉夫自此再未见过她。 没家没妈，伊斯拉夫不知所措。虽然他已经习惯了德鲁丝芭小屋里寒冷的露天环境，但他饿得紧。 “能给我块肉吗？”他询问街上的屠夫。“我饿极了。” 屠夫已经认识这个男孩好多年了，经常对他的妻子说他很同情这个孩子，在一个没有天花板和墙的家中长大。于是他对着伊斯拉夫笑了笑说：“滚。小心我揍你。” 伊斯拉夫赶紧远离屠夫，来到附近的一家酒馆。酒馆掌柜曾经是王廷里的贴身男仆，他知道这男孩是个王子。他也不只一次在街上看到这衣衫褴褛的可怜小家伙，哀叹命运对他的不公。 “我能吃点东西吗？”伊斯拉夫求这位老板。“我太饿了。” “没把你炖了就是你走运了。”酒馆掌柜答。 伊斯拉夫赶紧离开酒馆。那天接下来的时间里，男孩乞求了许多埃罗尔嘉德的正直公民，请他们给口吃的。一个人扔了点东西给他、但却只是一块不能果腹的石头。 夜幕降临，一个衣衫褴褛的男人走到伊斯拉夫眼前，一言不发地给了他一块水果和一片肉干。小家伙睁大眼睛接过它狼吞虎咽起来。他亲切地感谢了这个男人。 “要是明天再让我看见你在街上要饭，”男人低声咆哮道，“我就亲手宰了你。这镇上我们帮只准有这么多乞丐，你一来人就太多了。你在砸我们的饭碗。” 所幸伊斯拉夫知道怎么跑路。那天他跑了个一整夜。 欲知伊斯拉夫传奇后事如何，请待《盗贼》分解。

THE RED KITCHEN READER By Simocles Quo

hough naturally modest, I must admit to some pleasure in being dubbed by our Emperor's father, the late Pelagius IV, as "the finest connoisseur in Tamriel." He was also good enough to appoint me the first, and to this day, the only Master of Cuisine in the Imperial Court. Other Emperors, of course, had master chefs and cooks in their staff, but only during the reign of Pelagius was there someone of rarefied tastes to plan the menus and select the finest produce to be served at court. His son Uriel requested that I continue in that position, but I was forced to graciously decline the invitation, because of age and poor health. This book, however, is not intended to be autobiography. I have had a great many adventures in my life as a knight of fine dining, but my intention for this book is much more specific. Many times I have been asked, "What is the best thing you ever ate?" The answer to that is not a simple one. Much of the pleasure of a great meal is not only in the food: it is in the setting, the company, the mood. Eat an indifferently cooked roast or a simple stew with your one true love, and it is a meal to be remembered. Have an excellent twelve-course feast with dull company, while feeling slightly ill, and it will be forgotten, or remembered only with distaste. Sometimes meals are memorable for the experiences that come before them. Fairly recently, in northern Skyrim, I had a bit of bad luck. I was with a group of fishermen, observing their technique of capturing a very rare, very delicious fish called Merringar. The fish is found only far from shore, so it was a week's voyage out beyond civilization. Well, we found our school of Merringar, but as the fishermen began spearing them, the blood in the water attracted a family of Dreugh, who capsized the boat and everyone on it. I managed to save myself, but the fishermen and all our supplies were lost. Sailing is not, alas, a skill I have picked up over the years, and it took me three weeks, with no provisions, to find my way back to the kingdom of Solitude. I had managed to catch enough small fish to eat raw, but I was still delirious from hunger and thirst. The first meal I had on shore, of Nordic roast boar, Jazbay wine, and, yes, filet of Merringar would have been excellent under any circumstances, but because of the threat of starvation I had faced, it was divine beyond words. Sometimes meals are even memorable for the experiences that follow them. In a tavern in Falinesti, I was introduced to a simple peasant dish called Kollopi, delicious little balls of flesh, thick with spices and juice, so savory I asked the proprietress whence they came. Mother Pascost explained that the Kollopi were an arboreal rodent that fed exclusively on the most tender branches of the graht-oak, and I was fortunate enough to be in Valenwood at the time of the annual harvest. I was invited to join with a small colony of Imga monkeys, who alone could gather these succulent little mice. Because they lived only on the slenderest branches of the trees, and only on the ends of those same branches, the Imga had to climb beneath them and jump up to "pick" the Kollopi from their perches. Imga are, of course, naturally dexterous, but I was then relatively young and spry, and they let me help them. While I could never jump as high they could, with practice, I found that if I kept my head and upper body rigid, and launched off the ground with a scissors-like kick, I could reach the Kollopi on the lowest branches of the tree. I believe I gathered three Kollopi myself, though with considerable effort. To this day, I salivate at the thought of Kollopi, but my mind is on the image of myself and several dozen Imgas leaping around beneath the shade of the graht-oaks. Then, of course, there are the rare meals memorable for what came before, after, and during the meal, which brings me to the finest thing I ever ate, the meal that began my lifelong obsession with excellent cuisine. As a child growing up in Cheydinhal, I did not care for food at all. I recognized the value of nutrition, for I was not a complete dullard, but I cannot say that mealtime brought me any pleasure at all. Partly, of course, this was the fault of my family's cook, who believed that spices were an invention of the Daedra, and that good Imperials should like their food boiled, textureless and flavorless. Though I think she was alone in assigning a religious significance to this, my sampling of traditional Cyrodilic cuisine suggests that the philosophy is regrettably common in my homeland. Though I did not enjoy food per se, I was not a morose, unadventurous child in other respects. I enjoyed the fights in the Arena, of course, and nothing made me happier than wandering the streets of my town, with my imagination as my only companion. It was on one such jaunt on a sunny Fredas in Mid Year that I made a discovery that changed my heart and my life. There were several old abandoned houses down the street from my own home, and I often played around them, imagining them to be filled with desperate outlaws or haunted by hundreds of evil spirits. I never had the nerve to go inside. In fact, had I not that day seen some other children who had delighted in teasing me in the past, I would never have gone in. But I needed a sanctuary, so I ran into the closest one. The house seemed to be as desolate on the inside as on the outside, further proof that no one lived there, and had not for some time. When I heard footsteps, I could only assume that the loathsome little urchins I hoped to avoid had followed me in. I escaped to the basement, and from there, past a broken-down wall that led to a well. I could still hear the footsteps above, and I decided that I was still loath to confront my tormentors. Knocking aside the rusty locks on the well, I slipped down below. The well was dry, but I discovered it was far from empty. There was a sort of a sub-basement to the house, three large rooms that were clean, furnished, and evidently not abandoned at all. My senses told me someone was living in the house, after all: not only my sense of sight, but my sense of smell. For one of the rooms was a large red-painted kitchen, and spread out on the coals of the oven was a roast, carved into small morsels. Passing a beautiful and appropriate bas-relief of a mother carving a roast for her grateful children, I beheld the kitchen and the wonders within. Like I said, food had never interested me before, but I was transfixed, and even now as I write this, words fail me in describing the rich aroma that hung in the air. It was like nothing I had ever smelled in my family's kitchen, and I was unable to stop myself from popping one of the steaming chunks of meat into my mouth. The taste was magical, the flesh tender and sweet. Before I knew it, I had eaten everything on the stove, and I learned at that very second the truth that that food can and should be sublime. After gorging myself and having my culinary epiphany, I was conflicted on what to do. Part of me wanted to wait down in that red kitchen until the chef returned, so I could ask him what his secret recipe was for the delicious meat. Part of me recognized that I had stolen into someone's house and eaten their dinner, and it would be wise to leave while I could. That was what I did. Time and again, I've tried to return to that strange, wonderful place, but Cheydinhal has changed over time. Old houses have been reclaimed, and new houses abandoned. I know what to look for on the inside of the house - the well, the beautiful etching of a woman preparing to carve out a roast for her children, the red kitchen itself - but I have never been able to find the house again. After a while, as I grew older, I stopped trying. It is better as it remains in my memory, the most perfect meal I ever ate. The inspiration for my life that followed all was cooked up, together with that fabulous meat, right there in the Red Kitchen.

虽然我生性谦逊，但必须承认，能被先皇佩拉吉奥斯四世称为“泰姆瑞尔最好的品鉴师”，我还是非常高兴的。他还任命我为帝国宫廷中第一位，也是至今唯一的“烹调大师”。当然，其他皇帝也有厨师，但只有在佩拉吉奥斯时期，才有品味高雅的人负责制定菜单，甄选食材以供养宫廷。他的儿子尤瑞尔陛下要求我继续担当此职位，奈何我年事已高，不再康健，只得拒绝了这一邀请。 但此书不是自传。身为美食界的骑士，我一生冒险无数，但我写本书的意图要更具体。经常有人问我：“你吃过最好吃的东西是什么？” 想回答这个问题并不容易。一顿大餐的快乐不止在于食物本身，还关乎环境、同伴还有心情。和你的心上人吃一顿平淡无奇的烤肉或者简简单单的炖菜，也是一顿值得铭记的大餐。和闷葫芦吃一顿十二菜大宴，也会让你感到不适，进而遗忘，或者每次想起都不禁厌恶。 有时，一顿饭会因为用餐前的经历而难以忘怀。 不久前，我在天际北部碰上了一件倒霉事。当时我与一群渔民同行，观摩他们捕捉一种稀有鲜美的鱼—“梅里加”。这种鱼只在远离海岸的地方才能找到，所以要航行一周，远离文明。我们顺利找到了梅里加鱼群，但当渔民们开始用长矛刺鱼时，水里的血吸引了一群蟹灵，它们把船弄翻，人都落到了水里。我设法自救，但渔民与所有补给全都葬身大海。哎，我向来不擅航海，在没有补给的情况下，我花了三周才找到了回独孤王国的路。我设法捉了些能够生吃的小鱼，但还是因为又饥又渴而神志不清。上岸后第一餐，诺德烤猪排、贾兹贝葡萄酒，再配上，没错，梅里加鱼排。这东西寻常时已是珍馐，备受饥饿之苦后品尝，滋味更是超凡脱俗，难以言表。 有时，一顿饭甚至会因随之而来的经历而难忘。 在法林纳斯提的一家小酒馆，有人给我介绍了一道简单的农家菜，叫做“科罗皮”，是种美味的小肉丸，里面配着浓稠的香料和酱汁，十分的美味，我就问店主，这些肉丸是哪里来的。帕斯科斯特大娘解释说，科罗皮是一种树栖啮齿动物，只吃橡树最鲜嫩的枝叶，而我正好赶上一年一度的收获季来到威伦森林，实属幸运。这种肥美的小老鼠只有因迦猴子能够捕捉，我受邀同它们一同行动。这些小老鼠住在树稍最细的树枝的末端，因迦得爬到树下，跳起来把科罗皮“摘”下来。当然，因迦天生就很灵巧，但那时我还相对年轻，精力充沛，它们就让我也搭把手。虽然我跳不了他们那么高，但经过练习，只要保持头部和上半身不动，然后像剪刀一样蹬地，我就能够到最低树枝上的科罗皮了。我费了好一番力气，最终亲手捉到三只。 直到今天，一想到科罗皮，我就会流口水。但脑海里挥之不去的，却是自己和几十只因迦在橡树下蹦蹦跳跳的画面。 当然，世上还有更难得的体验：有时，一顿饭之所以令人难忘，是因为从餐前到餐后发生的一切。这就要说到我吃过的最棒的一餐了，正是从这一餐开始，我一生都对美食痴迷不已。 我自幼在夏丁赫尔，根本不喜欢美食。毕竟我不是个傻子，当然知道营养的价值，但用餐从未给我带来过任何欢乐。这一定程度上要怪我们家的厨子，她觉得香料是迪德拉的发明，优秀的帝国人应该喜欢没有质地没有味道单纯煮熟的食物。虽然我以为只有她一个人会给这事安上宗教意义，直到后来我尝过一些传统的希罗帝尔菜肴，才发现这种理念在我故乡可能相当普遍。 虽说我不爱吃东西，但儿时的我并不沉闷孤僻，也乐于探索新鲜事物。我当然喜欢看竞技场里的战斗，但最让我开心的，莫过于独自漫步城中街巷、任由思绪天马行空。就在年中月某个晴朗的周五，我像往常一样出门闲逛，那次发现彻底改写了我的心境与人生。 在我家附近的街道上有几座废弃的老屋，我经常在周围玩耍，想象着它们里面挤满了绝望的亡命之徒，或者纠缠着成百上千的恶灵。我从来没有勇气进去。事实上，如果那天不是遇见了几个喜欢取笑我的孩子，我永远也不会进去。但我需要一个避难所，所以我就进了离我最近的一个。 这所房子的里里外外都显得很荒凉，进一步证明了这里没有人住过，而且是很长一段时间了。可我听见了脚步声，我以为是我不想碰到的那些混小子跟着我进来了。我逃进了地下室，又从那儿穿过一面破墙，来到了一口井边。我仍然可以听到上面的脚步声，也不愿意面对那些霸凌者。所以我拨开井上生锈的锁，溜了下去。 井虽然干涸，但我发现它里面别有洞天。房子里有一个类似地下室的地方，足足有三个大房间，干净整洁，摆放家具，显然不是遗弃已久的样子。我觉得这儿就是有人居住的，不光眼睛看出来了，鼻子也闻出来了。因为其中一间屋子是漆着红漆的大厨房，在炉子的煤块上铺着一份切成小块的烤肉。我路过一幅漂亮又应景的浮雕，雕的是一位母亲正在为满怀感恩的孩子们切烤肉，然后我看清了那间厨房，还有里面的奇迹。 如先前所言，我早年对吃的根本没兴趣，但那一刻我却被牢牢吸引住了。即使现在我写这篇文章，也无法用语言来描述空气中弥漫的浓郁香气。我从未在我家厨房里闻到这样的味道，忍不住把一块冒着热气的肉塞进嘴里。味道很神奇，肉又嫩又甜。等我回过神来，我已经把炉子上的所有东西都吃完了，就在那一刻，我才明白一个道理：食物，可以是——也应当是——极致的享受。 在狼吞虎咽、顿悟了美食的真谛后，我反而不知该如何是好了。我有点想在那红色厨房里等待厨师回来，询问他美味烤肉的秘方。但我也意识到，我是闯进了别人的房子，吃了他们的晚餐，所以趁还能脱身时赶紧走才是明智之举。我就这么离开了。 我曾一次又一次试图回到那奇怪而美好的地方，但随着时间的推移，夏丁赫尔变化很大，不断有旧房住新人，也不断有新居变空屋。我知道应该在房子里找什么--井、女人为孩子切肉的浮雕、红色的厨房，但我再也没能找到那所房子。时光流逝，年岁渐长，我停止了寻找。如此也好，让它留在我的记忆中，成为我吃过最完美的一餐。 我此后人生的所有灵感，和那顿绝妙的美味烤肉一样，都是在那间红色厨房烹制而出。

other Pascost disappeared into the sordid hole that was her tavern, and emerged a moment later with a scrap of paper with Liodes Jurus's familiar scrawl. Decumus Scotti held it up before a patch of sunlight that had found its way through the massive boughs of the tree city, and read. Sckotti, So you made it to Falinnesti, Vallinwood! Congradulatens! Im sure you had quit a adventure getting here. Unfortonitly, Im not here anymore as you probaby guess. Theres a town down rivver called Athie Im at. Git a bote and join me! Its ideal! I hope you brot a lot of contracks, cause these peple need a lot of building done. They wer close to the war, you see, but not so close they dont have any mony left to pay. Ha ha. Meat me down here as son as you can. Jurus So, Scotti pondered, Jurus had left Falinesti and gone to some place called Athie. Given his poor penmanship and ghastly spelling, it could equally well be Athy, Aphy, Othry, Imthri, Urtha, or Krakamaka. The sensible thing to do, Scotti knew, was to call this adventure over and try to find some way to get back home to the Imperial City. He was no mercenary devoted to a life of thrills: he was, or at least had been, a senior clerk at a successful private building commission. Over the last few weeks, he had been robbed by the Cathay-Raht, taken on a death march through the jungle by a gang of giggling Bosmeri, half-starved to death, drugged with fermented pig's milk, nearly slain by some kind of giant tick, and attacked by archers. He was filthy, exhausted, and had, he counted, ten gold pieces to his name. Now the man whose proposal brought him to the depths of misery was not even there. It was both judicious and seemly to abandon the enterprise entirely. And yet, a small but distinct voice in his head told him: You have been chosen. You have no other choice but to see this through. Scotti turned to the stout old woman, Mother Pascost, who had been watching him curiously: "I was wondering if you knew of a village that was at the edge of the recent conflict with Elsweyr. It's called something like Ath-ie?" "You must mean Athay," she grinned. "My middle lad, Viglil, he manages a dairy down there. Beautiful country, right on the river. Is that where your friend went?" "Yes," said Scotti. "Do you know the fastest way to get there?" After a short conversation, an even shorter ride to Falinesti's roots by way of the platforms, and a jog to the river bank, Scotti was negotiating transport with a huge fair-haired Bosmer with a face like a pickled carp. He called himself Captain Balfix, but even Scotti with his sheltered life could recognize him for what he was. A retired pirate for hire, a smuggler for certain, and probably much worse. His ship, which had clearly been stolen in the distant past, was a bent old Imperial sloop. "Fifty gold and we'll be in Athay in two days time," boomed Captain Balfix expansively. "I have ten, no, sorry, nine gold pieces," replied Scotti, and feeling the need for explanation, added, "I had ten, but I gave one to the Platform Ferryman to get me down here." "Nine is just as fine," said the captain agreeably. "Truth be told, I was going to Athay whether you paid me or not. Make yourself comfortable on the boat, we'll be leaving in just a few minutes." Decumus Scotti boarded the vessel, which sat low in the water of the river, stacked high with crates and sacks that spilled out of the hold and galley and onto the deck. Each was marked with stamps advertising the most innocuous substances: copper scraps, lard, ink, High Rock meal (marked "For Cattle"), tar, fish jelly. Scotti's imagination reeled picturing what sorts of illicit imports were truly aboard. It took more than those few minutes for Captain Balfix to haul in the rest of his cargo, but in an hour, the anchor was up and they were sailing downriver towards Athay. The green gray water barely rippled, only touched by the fingers of the breeze. Lush plant life crowded the banks, obscuring from sight all the animals that sang and roared at one another. Lulled by the serene surroundings, Scotti drifted to sleep. At night, he awoke and gratefully accepted some clean clothes and food from Captain Balfix. "Why are you going to Athay, if I may ask?" queried the Bosmer. "I'm meeting a former colleague there. He asked me to come down from the Imperial City where I worked for the Atrius Building Commission to negotiate some contracts," Scotti took another bite of the dried sausages they were sharing for dinner. "We're going to try to repair and refurbish whatever bridges, roads, and other structures that got damaged in the recent war with the Khajiiti." "It's been a hard two years," the captain nodded his head. "Though I suppose good for me and the likes of you and your friend. Trade routes cut off. Now they think there's going to be war with the Summurset Isles, you heard that?" Scotti shook his head. "I've done my share of smuggling skooma down the coast, even helping some revolutionary types escape the Mane's wrath, but now the wars've made me a legitimate trader, a business-man. The first casualties of war is always the corrupted." Scotti said he was sorry to hear that, and they lapsed into silence, watching the stars and moons' reflection on the still water. The next day, Scotti awoke to find the captain wrapped up in his sail, torpid from alcohol, singing in a low, slurred voice. When he saw Scotti rise, he offered his flagon of jagga. "I learned my lesson during revelry at western cross." The captain laughed, and then burst into tears, "I don't want to be legitimate. Other pirates I used to know are still raping and stealing and smuggling and selling nice folk like you into slavery. I swear to you, I never thought the first time that I ran a real shipment of legal goods that my life would turn out like this. Oh, I know, I could go back to it, but Baan Dar knows not after all I've seen. I'm a ruined man." Scotti helped the weeping mer out of the sail, murmuring words of reassurance. Then he added, "Forgive me for changing the subject, but where are we?" "Oh," moaned Captain Balfix miserably. "We made good time. Athay's right around the bend in the river." "Then it looks like Athay's on fire," said Scotti, pointing. A great plume of smoke black as pitch was rising above the trees. As they drifted around the bend, they next saw the flames, and then the blackened skeletal remains of the village. Dying, blazing villagers leapt from rocks into the river. A cacophony of wailing met their ears, and they could see, roaming along the edges of the town, the figures of Khajiiti soldiers bearing torches. "Baan Dar bless me!" slurred the captain. "The war's back on!" "Oh, no," whimpered Scotti. The sloop drifted with the current toward the opposite shore away from the fiery town. Scotti turned his attention there, and the sanctuary it offered. Just a peaceful arbor, away from the horror. There was a shudder of leaves in two of the trees and a dozen lithe Khajiit dropped to the ground, armed with bows. "They see us," hissed Scotti. "And they've got bows!" "Well, of course they have bows," snarled Captain Balfix. "We Bosmer may have invented the bloody things, but we didn't think to keep them secret, you bloody bureaucrat." "Now, they're setting their arrows on fire!" "Yes, they do that sometimes." "Captain, they're shooting at us! They're shooting at us with flaming arrows!" "Ah, so they are," the captain agreed. "The aim here is to avoid being hit." But hit they were, and very shortly thereafter. Even worse, the second volley of arrows hit the supply of pitch, which ignited in a tremendous blue blaze. Scotti grabbed Captain Balfix and they leapt overboard just before the ship and all its cargo disintegrated. The shock of the cold water brought the Bosmer into temporary sobriety. He called to Scotti, who was already swimming as fast as he could toward the bend. "Master Decumus, where do you think you're swimming to?" "Back to Falinesti!" cried Scotti. "It will take you days, and by the time you get there, everyone will know about the attack on Athay! They'll never let anyone they don't know in! The closest village downriver is Grenos, maybe they'll give us shelter!" Scotti swam back to the captain and side-by-side they began paddling in the middle of the river, past the burning residuum of the village. He thanked Mara that he had learned to swim. Many a Cyrodiil did not, as largely land-locked as the Imperial Province was. Had he been raised in Mir Corrup or Artemon, he might have been doomed, but the Imperial City itself was encircled by water, and every lad and lass there knew how to cross without a boat. Even those who grew up to be clerks and not adventurers. Captain Balfix's sobriety faded as he grew used to the water's temperature. Even in wintertide, the Xylo River was fairly temperate and after a fashion, even comfortable. The Bosmer's strokes were uneven, and he'd stray closer to Scotti and then further away, pushing ahead and then falling behind. Scotti looked to the shore to his right: the flames had caught the trees like tinder. Behind them was an inferno, with which they were barely keeping pace. To the shore on their left, all looked fair, until he saw a tremble in the river-reeds, and then what caused it. A pride of the largest cats he had ever seen. They were auburn-haired, green-eyed beasts with jaws and teeth to match his wildest nightmares. And they were watching the two swimmers, and keeping pace. "Captain Balfix, we can't go to either that shore or the other one, or we'll be parboiled or eaten," Scotti whispered. "Try to even your kicking and your strokes. Breath like you would normally. If you're feeling tired, tell me, and we'll float on our backs for a while." Anyone who has had the experience of giving rational advice to a drunkard would understand the hopelessness. Scotti kept pace with the captain, slowing himself, quickening, drifting left and right, while the Bosmer moaned old ditties from his pirate days. When he wasn't watching his companion, he watched the cats on the shore. After a stretch, he turned to his right. Another village had caught fire. Undoubtedly, it was Grenos. Scotti stared at the blazing fury, awed by the sight of the destruction, and did not hear that the captain had ceased to sing. When he turned back, Captain Balfix was gone. Scotti dove into the murky depths of the river over and over again. There was nothing to be done. When he surfaced after his final search, he saw that the giant cats had moved on, perhaps assuming that he too had drowned. He continued his lonely swim downriver. A tributary, he noted, had formed a final barrier, keeping the flames from spreading further. But there were no more towns. After several hours, he began to ponder the wisdom of going ashore. Which shore was the question. He was spared the decision. Ahead of him was a rocky island with a bonfire. He did not know if he were intruding on a party of Bosmeri or Khajiiti, only that he could swim no more. With straining, aching muscles, he pulled himself onto the rocks. They were Bosmer refugees he gathered, even before they told him. Roasting over the fire was the remains of one of the giant cats that had been stalking him through the jungle on the opposite shore. "Senche-Tiger," said one of the young warriors ravenously. "It's no animal -- it's as smart as any Cathay-Raht or Ohmes or any other bleeding Khajiiti. Pity this one drowned. I would have gladly killed it. You'll like the meat, though. Sweet, from all the sugar these asses eat." Scotti did not know if he was capable of eating a creature as intelligent as a man or mer, but he surprised himself, as he had done several times over the last days. It was rich, succulent, and sweet, like sugared pork, but no seasonings had been added. He surveyed the crowd as he ate. A sad lot, some still weeping for lost family members. They were the survivors of both the villages of Grenos and Athay, and war was on every person's lips. Why had the Khajiiti attacked again? Why -- specifically directed at Scotti, as a Cyrodiil -- why was the Emperor not enforcing peace in his provinces? "I was to meet another Cyrodiil," he said to a Bosmer maiden who he understood to be from Athay. "His name was Liodes Jurus. I don't suppose you know what might have happened to him." "I don't know your friend, but there were many Cyrodiils in Athay when the fire came," said the girl. "Some of them, I think, left quickly. They were going to Vindisi, inland, in the jungle. I am going there tomorrow, so are many of us. If you wish, you may come as well." Decumus Scotti nodded solemnly. He made himself as comfortable as he could in the stony ground of the river island, and somehow, after much effort, he fell asleep. But he did not sleep well.

帕斯寇斯特老妈消失在了酒馆肮脏的坑洞里，过了一会儿又带着一小片有着利奥德斯·朱鲁斯凌乱字迹的碎纸片出现了。在阳光穿透树城巨大的枝条之前，戴奎莫斯·斯科提拿起信纸，读了起来。 斯哥提： 看来你已经成功抵达威抡森林的法里乃斯提了！恭喜啊！我很确定，你经历了好大一番波折才来到这的。可呀，事实和你可能菜的不太一样了，我现在不留在这了。这里月一座位于何流下游的城镇，名字叫诶俟西，我就在这。高一艘沿，然后过来和我一起干吧！这佷符合理想！我希望你多代些奇约过来，因为这些壬要修很多建筑物。他们大战在急，你也看到了，但是还没有紧张到他们没有积畜来消费的地步。哈哈。尽块来下游这里见我吧。 朱鲁斯 斯科提思索着，朱鲁斯已经离开了法林纳斯提，并且去了某个名为诶俟西的地方。考虑到他寒碜的笔迹和惨不忍睹的拼写，那里也非常有可能是叫作埃希、艾菲、欧塞瑞、乌尔萨、或者干脆卡拉卡马卡。斯科提知道，当下明智的做法是结束这场冒险，并且找到返回帝都老家的办法。他不是那些过着惊险日子的佣兵：他是，或者起码曾经是，隶属于一家功成名就的私人制建筑委会的高级文员。在过去的几个星期里，他曾被卡塞-拉特劫掠；在一伙傻笑个不停的波斯莫带领下，踏上了一场生死行军，饥困潦倒险些化作饿殍；喝下发酵的猪乳而醉倒；几乎丧命于某种巨型蜱虫，还被一群弓手们围攻攒射。他如今已蓬头垢面、疲乏劳顿，并且在他数过后，他手里只有十枚金币了。现在，这个给过他一项令他深陷困厄苦痛深渊的提议的男人，甚至都不在这里。全数放弃掉这门生意是既理智且合理的选择。 然而， 一道细微却清晰可闻的声音在他脑海里告诉他：命运已经选中了你。除了看清眼前一切，你没有别的退路。 斯科提转向了那个体态敦实、正好奇地端详着他的老妪，帕斯寇斯特老妈：“我想知道，你是否知道一座最近正处于和艾斯维尔冲突边缘的村庄。它的名字是类似‘诶俟-西’之类的？” “你肯定说的是艾赛，”她龇牙笑道，“我家里排行中间的儿子，维格里尔，他在那个地处下游的地方经营着一家小商铺。风光秀丽的乡村，就位于河岸上。你的朋友是去了那吗？” “是的。”斯科提说，“你知道前往那里的最快路线吗？” 一番短暂的交谈之后，斯科提快马加鞭，乘坐升降平台到达法林纳斯提根系，一路小跑着来到河岸，随后他和一位满头黄发、面如腌鲤鱼的高大波斯莫商讨起了交通问题。他自称巴尔菲克斯船长，但即使是坐惯了办公室的斯科提也能一眼认出他的身份。待雇佣的退休海盗，身份确凿的走私者，此外很有可能还会有更糟的情况。他那艘明显是一艘歪七扭八的老旧帝国单桅帆船，显然是很久以前偷到手的。 “五十枚金币，我们两天内到艾赛。”巴尔菲克斯船长声音低沉而不失豪爽地说道。 “我只有十，不，抱歉，九枚金币了。”斯科提回答道，他觉得有必要解释一下，于是补充道，“我有十枚金币，但是我给了平台渡夫一枚，好让我下到这来。” “九枚也成。”队长欣然接受道，“说实话，不管你付钱与否，我都是要去艾赛的。在船上请别客气，我们几分钟内就出发。” 戴奎莫斯·斯科提上了船，船体吃水颇深，满载着累叠的板条箱，以及积满了船舱和厨房、多到堆上甲板的麻袋。每一份货物都被打上了表明了它们不过是最人畜无害的货物的印记：碎铜片、猪油、墨水、高岩谷粉饲料（标记有“饲养牛用”）、沥青、鱼肉冻。斯科提脑中想象力一阵发散，揣度起何种违禁物品是真的运上了船。 巴尔菲克斯船长花了好几分钟来拖拽完余下的货物，一小时不到，船锚升起，他们已经沿河驶向了艾赛。幽绿的河面几乎波澜不惊，仅仅触着几缕微风的轻抚。夹岸草木纷繁而生，掩映着百兽啼鸣、彼此呼唤的景致。四面的幽静景观安抚了斯科提的内心，他不知不觉中进入了梦乡。 是夜，他苏醒过来，满怀感激地从巴尔菲克斯船长那收下了一些干净的衣服和食物。 “容我多问一句，你为什么要去艾赛呢？”波斯莫发出疑问。 “我要去那见一位前同事。他让我从我曾经工作的地方、阿特里乌斯建筑委会所在的帝都南下，来协商某些合约，”斯科提又咬了一口他们晚餐分食的干香肠，“我们想试试修复重建各类桥梁、道路还有其它最近在和卡吉特的交战中受波及的建筑。” “那两年过得很艰难。”船长点了点头，“不过这对你我还有你的朋友来说是有利的。商路也被截断了，现在他们觉得这里和夏暮岛也开战在即，你听说了吗？” 斯科提摇头以应。 “我做过沿岸走私斯库玛的活计，甚至还帮助过某类算是革命者的人逃脱鬃鬣的怒火，但现在战争已经让我变成了一个正规合法的商贩，一个生意人。战争首当其冲的牺牲品永远是堕落的人。” 斯科提真切地告诉了船长，他对听到这些内容深表遗憾。他们之间的夜谈渐渐转向了沉默，一同注视着宁静水面映出的星光月影。第二天，当斯科提醒来时，他看见船长已经回到了自己的舱室，穿上了衣服，还带着酒醉后慵懒的余韵，浅浅地低吟着一首调子。当他瞧见斯科提起身，便主动递了一瓶夹嘎给他。 “我已经在西十字路口的狂欢里学到教训了。” 船长大笑出声，接着突然痛哭流涕：“我不想这么规规矩矩。我过去认识的其他海盗现在还在肆意奸盗掳掠，大兴走私，拐卖你这样的好人去充作奴隶。我和你发誓，我从没想过我头一次真正跑了趟运载合法物资的航运，我的生活竟然变成了这副模样。噢，我知道，我可以重返过去的生活，但是连班·达尔也不知晓我所经历过的一切。我已经一无所有了。” 斯科提帮扶着这个哭泣的莫走出了舱室，他还兀自喃喃自语着说服自己。接着，斯科提补充道：“请原谅我转移话题，但是，我们现在是在哪？” “哦。”巴尔菲克斯船长哀号一声，“我们出来的正是时候。艾赛就在前方河流弯道一带。” “不过艾赛好像失火了。”斯科提指着前方问道。 一股如沥青般黑色的浓烟，自树丛中升腾而上。随着他们行船转过弯，入眼便是重重火光，之后是燎作焦黑的椽桁梁柱。奄奄一息的村民们身着烈火，从岩石上跃入河中。他们耳中听见一阵凄惶的嚎哭，同时还看见卡吉特兵卒手持火炬的身影沿着市镇边缘走动。 “班·达尔保佑我！”船长低声祈祷着，“又开始打仗了！” “哦，不，”斯科提抽噎着喊道。 单桅帆船顺流而行，远离了暴乱中的城镇，驶向对岸。斯科提将注意力转向了那里，并注意到了它提供的庇护区域。只要是一片树林，能够远离战乱带来的恐惧就好。树林之间，有两棵树木的树叶微微颤动，接着一伙身形灵活柔韧的卡吉特，人人挎弓，从树中跳出，轻巧落地。 “他们看见我们了，”斯科提带着嘶嘶的尾音说道，“他们还带了弓。” “废话，他们肯定有弓。”巴尔菲克斯船长怒喝道，“或许是我们波斯莫发明出了这些利器，但我们可从未想过要将它们秘而不宣，你这该死的狗官！” “他们在往箭上点火！” “没错，他们有时候会这么做。” “船长，他们在向我们放箭！他们在用火箭射我们！” “啊，他们就是这样。”船长表示同意，“现在首要目标是别中箭。” 但片刻之后，他们还是被箭矢射中。更糟的是，第二轮箭雨点燃了船上的沥青补给品，燃烧成一片青蓝火海。斯科提紧紧抓住巴尔菲克斯船长，在船身解体、货物尽毁之前从船上跳入水里。冰寒的水温带来的刺激让波斯莫暂时冷静了下来。他呼唤着斯科提的名字，而斯科提已经竭尽全速地游向了弯道处。 “戴奎莫斯老板，你现在是要游到哪去？” “回到法林纳斯提！”斯科提大叫道。 “那得花上好几天，而且在你到达那里之前，所有人都会知道艾赛遇袭的事！他们不会放任何未确认身份的人进入的！下游最近的村庄是格仁诺斯，或许他们会给我们提供庇护。” 斯科提游回到船长身边，两人在河心拨动着河水，并肩而游，经过了村墟燃烧的残迹。感谢玛拉，他还学会了游泳。鉴于希罗帝尔行省大部分地区处于内陆，许多希罗帝尔人并不会这一技能。要是他生养于米尔·克洛普或者阿尔特蒙，自己可能已经溺亡水中。但是帝都自身却是被水流环抱，因此那里的每一位少年男女都知道如何不凭舟楫而绝江河的方法。甚至是那些成年后做了文职人员而非冒险者的人也颇通水性。 随着身体逐渐适应了水温，巴尔菲克斯船长的冷静褪去了。即使是在冬季，西洛河的水温也相当温和，甚至能勉强说得上舒适。这个波斯莫在水中四肢乱划，和斯科提之间时远时近，有时游到他身前，有时又落在了后面。 斯科提看着他右侧的河岸：火舌附着延烧于树木，如引线被点燃一般，在树木掩映的后方，光焰大作，火势蔓延的速度几乎不能追及他们。在自己左侧的岸上，一切似乎都归于平静，直到他看见有什么物事在芦苇丛中一阵颤动，以及那阵颤动的发出者。那是一群他此生所见的最大的巨猫。这群野兽生着赤褐色绒毛与绿色的瞳孔，有着与他最疯狂的噩梦如出一辙的尖牙利爪。它们不紧不慢地缀在他们身边，紧盯着两个水里游泳的人。 “巴尔菲克斯船长，我们哪边都不能上岸，不然不是被烹煮得半熟，就是直接生吞活剥，”斯科提压低嗓子说道。“你得尽量让划水蹬水的动作协调一些。像你平时那样自然地呼吸。如果你觉得累了，就告诉我一声，我们可以仰躺着漂浮一会。” 任何一位有过对酒鬼讲道理的经历的人，都会明白这种无力感。斯科提保持着处在船长近侧，时而放缓速度，时而加快，随河水左右往复漂流，而与此同时，波斯莫呜咽着他当海盗时学来的小调。在斯科提盯着他同伴的空档中，他会看向岸上的猫。过了一段时间，他看向了右岸。另一座村庄也陷入火海。毫无疑问，这就是格仁诺斯。斯科提凝视着燃烧的火焰，为生灵涂炭的惨状而感叹，忽略了船长戛然而止的哼唱。 当他转过头来，巴尔菲克斯船长已经不见了。 斯科提一次又一次潜入了幽昏的深水中，然而每一次却无功而返。当他结束了最后一次搜寻，浮出水面后，他看见巨猫们已经离开，或许是巨猫们认为他也沉水溺亡了。他开始继续一个人独自沿河向下游去。他注意到一条支流形成了一道难以改变的阻隔，阻挡了火势进一步扩散。但是这里也不再有幸存下来的村镇。数小时后，他开始思考着登岸的念头。问题在于选择哪一处河岸。 之后，他用不着做决定了。在他前方是一座被人生起了篝火、乱石嶙峋的小岛。他不知道自己是否误入了一伙波斯莫或者卡吉特的聚会，只是他实在难以支撑着再游下去。伴着拉伤的肌肉阵阵疼痛，他迫使自己奋力靠向了岛屿的岩石。 甚至在对方开口告诉他之前，他便推测出他们是波斯莫难民。在火上烧烤的尸块，正属于之前在对岸丛林里紧跟他的巨猫中的一只。 “森祛虎。”年轻的战士们中，有人一面大快朵颐，一面说着。“它不是动物——这家伙和随便哪只卡塞-拉特，或者欧莫斯，或者其它该死的卡吉特一样狡猾。很可惜这头已经淹死了。我本来能痛快地宰掉它的。不过，你会喜欢这肉的。它尝起来很甜，这些蠢蛋太爱吃糖了。 斯科提不知道他是否能够吃掉一个同人或莫一般拥有智慧的生物，但是正如过去几天里，他已经做出了好几次让自己也瞠目结舌的举动了，这一次他也照做不误。虽然没有放任何调料，但是那肉吃起来却香味浓郁、美味多汁，还带着宛如裹着糖浆的猪肉一般的甜味。在他进食的同时，他环顾着周围的人群。众人一片悲戚，有些仍在为痛失亲人而垂泪哭泣。他们来自格仁诺斯和艾赛的幸存者，人人都在议论着战争。为什么卡吉特又发起了攻击？为什么——尤其在斯科提这位希罗帝尔人听来尤为刺耳——为什么帝国不以强权介入它的行省来迫使其维护和平？ “我想去见见另一个希罗帝尔人，”在得知了波斯莫少女来自艾赛后，他对她说道。“他的名字是利奥德斯·朱鲁斯。我不觉得你知道他身上可能发生了什么。” “我不认识你的朋友，但是火灾来袭时，艾赛确实有很多希罗帝尔人。”女孩说道，“他们中的一部分逃离得很快。他们去往了温蒂斯，就在内陆的丛林中。我明天就动身前去那里，我们中的大多数人也一样。如果你想的话，也可以一起来。” 戴奎莫斯·斯科提郑重地点了点头。在这片布满乱石的河中岛屿上，他尽可能地让自己感到舒适，不知怎的，费尽周折后终于睡了过去。但他睡得并不安稳。

The Ransom of Zarek Ancient Tales of the Dwemer Part I by Marobar Sul

[pagebreak]

alemmil stood in her garden and read the letter her servant had brought to her. The bouquet of joss roses in her hand fell to the ground. For a moment it was as if all birds had ceased to sing and a cloud had passed over the sky. Her carefully cultivated and structured haven seemed to flood over with darkness. "We have thy son," it read. "We will be in touch with thee shortly with our ransom demands." Zarek had never made it as far as Akgun after all. One of the brigands on the road, Orcs probably, or accursed Dunmer, must have seen his well-appointed carriage, and taken him hostage. Jalemmil clutched at a post for support, wondering if her boy had been hurt. He was but a student, not the sort to fight against well-armed men, but had they beaten him? It was more than a mother's heart could bear to imagine. "Don't tell me they sent the ransom note so quickly," called a family voice, and a familiar face appeared through the hedge. It was Zarek. Jalemmil hurried to embrace her boy, tears running down her face. "What happened?" she cried. "I thought thou had been kidnapped." "I was," said Zarek. "Three huge soaring Nords attacked by carriage on the Frimvorn Pass. Brothers, as I learned, named Mathais, Ulin, and Koorg. Thou should have seen these men, mother. Each one of them would have had trouble fitting through the front door, I can tell thee." "What happened?" Jalemmil repeated. "Were thou rescued?" "I thought about waiting for that, but I knew they'd send off a ransom note and I know how thou does worry. So I remembered what my mentor at Akgun always said about remaining calm, observing thy surroundings, and looking for thy opponent's weakness," Zarek grinned. "It took a while, though, because these fellows were truly monsters. And then, when I listened to them, bragging to one another, I realized that vanity was their weakness." "What did thou do?" "They had me chained at their camp in the woods not far from Cael, on a high knoll over-looking a wide river. I heard one of them, Koorg, telling the others that it would take the better part of an hour to swim across the river and back. They were nodding in agreement, when I spoke up. "'I could swim that river and back in thirty minutes,' I said. "'Impossible,' said Koorg. 'I can swim faster than a little whelp like thee.' "So it was agreed that we would dive off the cliff, swim to the center island, and return. As we went to our respective rocks, Koorg took it upon himself to lecture me about all the fine points of swimming. The importance of synchronized movements of the arms and legs for maximum speed. How essential it was to breathe after only third or fourth stroke, not too often to slow thyself down, but not too often to lose one's air. I nodded and agreed to all his fine points. Then we dove off the cliffs. I made it to the island and back in a little over an hour, but Koorg never returned. He had dashed his brains at the rocks at the base of the cliff. I had noticed the telltale undulations of underwater rocks, and had taken the diving rock on the right." "But thou returned?" asked Jalemmil, astounded. "Was that not then when thou escaped?" "It was too risky to escape then," said Zarek. "They could have easily caught me again, and I wasn't keen to be blamed for Koorg's disappearance. I said I did not know what happened to him, and after some searching, they decided he had forgotten about the race and had swum ashore to hunt for food. They could not see how I could have had anything to do with his disappearance, as fully visible as I was throughout my swim. The two brothers began making camp along the rocky cliff-edge, picking an ideal location so that I would not be able to escape. "One of the brothers, Mathais, began commenting on the quality of the soil and the gradual incline of the rock that circled around the bay below. Ideal, he said, for a foot race. I expressed my ignorance of the sport, and he was keen to give me details of the proper technique for running a race. He made absurd faces, showing how one must breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth; how to bend one's knees to the proper angle on the rise; the importance of sure foot placement. Most important, he explained, was that the runner keep an aggressive but not too strenuous pace if one intends to win. It is fine to run in second place through the race, he said, provided one has the willpower and strength to pull out in the end. "I was an enthusiastic student, and Mathais decided that we ought to run a quick race around the edge of the bay before night fell. Ulin told us to bring back some firewood when we came back. We began at once down the path, skirting the cliff below. I followed his advice about breath, gait, and foot placement, but I ran with all my power right from the start. Despite his much longer legs, I was a few paces ahead as we wound the first corner. "With his eyes on my back, Mathais did not see the gape in the rock that I jumped over. He plummeted over the cliff before he had a chance to cry out. I spent a few minutes gathering some twigs before I returned to Ulin at camp." "Now thou were just showing off," frowned Jalemmil. "Surely that would have been a good time to escape." "Thou might think so," agreed Zarek. "But thou had to see the topography -- a few large trees, and then nothing but shrubs. Ulin would have noticed my absence and caught up with me in no time, and I would have had a hard time explaining Mathais's absence. However, the brief forage around the area allowed me to observe some of the trees close up, and I could formulate my final plan. "When I got back to camp with a few twigs, I told Ulin that Mathais was slow coming along, dragging a large dead tree behind him. Ulin scoffed at his brother's strength, saying it would take him time to pull up a live tree by the roots and drop it on the bonfire. I expressed reasonable doubt. "'I'll show thee,' he said, ripping up a ten foot tall specimen effortlessly. "'But that's scarcely a sapling,' I objected. 'I thought thou could rip up a tree.' His eyes followed mine to a magnificent, heavy-looking one at the edge of the clearing. Ulin grabbed it and began to shake it with a tremendous force to loosen its roots from the dirt. With that, he loosened the hive from the uppermost branches, dropping it down onto his head. "That was when I made my escape, mother," said Zarek, in conclusion, showing a little schoolboy pride. "While Mathais and Koorg were at the base of the cliff, and Ulin was flailing about, engulfed by a swarm." Jalemmil embraced her son once again. Publisher's Note I was reluctant to publish the works of Marobar Sul, but when the University of Gwylim Press asked me to edit this edition, I decided to use this as an opportunity to set the record straight once and for all. Scholars do not agree on the exact date of Marobar Sul's work, but it is generally agreed that they were written by the playwright "Gor Felim," famous for popular comedies and romances during the Interregnum between the fall of the First Cyrodilic Empire and the rise of Tiber Septim. The current theory holds that Felim heard a few genuine Dwemer tales and adapted them to the stage in order to make money, along with rewritten versions of many of his own plays. Gor Felim created the persona of "Marobar Sul" who could translate the Dwemer language in order to add some sort of validity to the work and make it even more valuable to the gullible. Note that while "Marobar Sul" and his works became the subject of heated controversy, there are no reliable records of anyone actually meeting "Marobar Sul," nor was there anyone of that name employed by the Mages Guild, the School of Julianos, or any other intellectual institution. In any case, the Dwemer in most of the tales of "Marobar Sul" bear little resemblance to the fearsome, unfathomable race that frightened even the Dunmer, Nords, and Redguards into submission and built ruins that even now have yet to be understood.

扎雷克的赎金 锻莫远古故事 其一 马洛巴尔·苏 著

[pagebreak]

嘉莱缪呆呆地站在她的花园里阅读仆人呈给她的信件，手中那束馨香的乔斯玫瑰坠落尘埃。一时间，有如众鸟止啼，阴云经空。她精心栽培布建的自留地好像已经被阴霾吞没灭顶。 　　 “咱抓了你儿子，”信中写道，“等着，咱就来找你谈谈这茬的赎金要多少。” 　　 扎雷克未曾涉足比阿克贡更远的土地。想来是路途上的劫道者，或许是兽人，或许是天杀的丹莫，肯定是盯上他那驾精良的马车，就这样抓作人质。嘉莱缪紧紧攥住身侧梁柱，心中无比担忧爱子是否受到伤害。他不过是个学生，绝非能与全副武装的暴徒正面对决的人……他们有殴打他吗？这远远超出了一颗母亲的心想象的范畴。 　　 “别说是他们动作这么快，已经送来勒索信了吧，”一道由小听到大的声音说。随后一张熟悉的面孔自树篱后冒出来。那是扎雷克。嘉莱缪扑过去紧拥她的儿子，清泪止不住地从双颊潸然而下。 “究竟怎么了？”她哭道，“我还以为你被人绑架了。” 　　 “没错，”扎雷克答，“经过弗里姆沃恩隘口那会，三个人高马大的诺德人劫了马车。据我了解，他们哥仨叫马泰斯、乌林和酷尔戈。你没见过这三人太可惜了，妈妈。我敢说，他们当中随便挑一个过来都会卡死在我们家的前门里。” 　　 “那还发生了什么？”嘉莱缪问，“你被解救了？” “我考虑了静待救援，但我明白他们发来勒索信时你肯定很担心。我便回忆起我在阿克贡的导师常说的冷静思考，环顾四下，找出敌人的弱点，”扎雷克咧嘴一笑，“我花了很长时间摸索，那三个真的是怪物。后来在听见他们对拼吹牛时，我意识到自负便是他们那薄弱之处。” 　　 “那你接着做了什么？” 　　 “他们把我关在凯尔附近树林中的营地里，在一处临瞰着某条极宽的大河的高丘上，我听到酷尔戈对另两个说，在河里游个来回要花上大半个小时。他们点头附议。就在那时我出声了。 　　 “‘我三十分钟就能游个来回。’我说。 　　 “‘屁，’酷尔戈说，‘老子肯定比你这狗崽子快。’ 　　 “我们顺势约好一起在峭壁上跳下去，一路游去河心岛再返回。我们登上各自的起跳岩，酷尔戈自信满满，还指点我游泳的诀窍。比如协调摆动四肢获取最大速度的要点、每三或四下摆臂就换气的必要性。要把握频率，过多导致减速而过少导致窒息。我颔首附和他说的所有的重点，随后我们跳水坠崖。我到岛上游完来回就花了一个小时多一点，但酷尔戈再未回来。他在峭壁底部的岩床上撞碎了头。我在刚开始就已留意到水下露出的岩块了，所以故意选了右面的石头起跳。” 　　 “但你还回去啦？”嘉莱缪大为惊愕，“你不是那时逃脱的吗？” “在那时就贸然逃离太危险，”扎雷克说，“他们完全能轻松地再次逮到我，我绝不想让他们意识到酷尔戈的消失和我能扯上关系。我说我不知道他干嘛去了，于是他们找了一阵，最后断定他忘记了要比赛，游上岸去猎取食物了。他们看不出我与他的失踪有何干系，毕竟他们全程监视我的一举一动。兄弟俩就选择在岩边缘崖开始扎营，这是个让我难以逃跑的理想位置。 　　 “兄弟之一，马泰斯，开始对此地土质和环绕下方河湾的倾斜岩石评头论足。他说，这块地很适合赛跑。于是我表示出对该项运动的一无所知，他那好为人师的心性一动，开始传授我赛跑的正规技巧细节。他扮鬼脸地展示如何鼻纳口吐式呼吸、如何屈膝到正确角度再抬升、正确位移步伐的要诀云云。至关重要的，他解释说，想要获胜，需要保持气势，但步伐不可过快。赛跑时保持在第二位最佳，他说这能激发人最终的意志和体力。 　　 “我学得很有热情，于是马泰斯打定主意，应该赶在入夜前绕湾岸比一场快速赛跑。乌林嘱咐我们回程时捡点柴火。我们便自小径开始，绕行奔向崖底。我采纳了他关于呼吸，步伐和步位的忠告，但开头我便以冲刺速度奔跑。尽管他腿很长，我还是在第一个弯道时领先数步。 　　 “因为他眼睛紧盯着我的背，马泰斯无法看到我跳过的岩间断层。在他有机会高声惨叫前就掉下崖去了。返回乌林的营地前我还花了几分钟收集一些细枝。” 　　 “你这不过是在秀，”嘉莱缪蹙眉，“那时正是脱身的好机会。” 　　 “你或许说得没错，”扎雷克同意，“但也要看地势，除数棵大树外都是灌木丛。乌林会马上注意到我失踪了并抓我回去，我根本不说不清马泰斯去哪儿了。但弄点柴火，我就有一阵时间可以摸索这一带，定下最终计策。待我抱着一些树枝返至营地，我告知乌林，称马泰斯稍后会归来，背后还会拖着一棵大枯木。乌林讥讽他兄弟的体力，自称能连根倒拔一棵活生生的树再摔进营火。我顺势对此表露了合理的质疑。 　　 “‘我让你见识见识，’他说完就轻而易举地拔起一棵足有十尺高的树。 　　 “‘可那不过是区区小树，’我提出异议，‘我看你应该能拔棵大的。’ “他的目光跟随我的视线移到林间空地边缘，那有棵看着就很重的宏伟大树。乌林一把抓握住树干，以巨力摇晃好将树根自土层松开。但随即也晃松了树顶枝头的蜂巢，直直掉在了他的头上。 　　 “我便在那时脱身啦，妈妈，”扎雷克最后怀着带有些许童真的自豪总结道，“那时马泰斯和酷尔戈都还在崖底，至于乌林？他在一大伙把他淹没的蜜蜂群里挣扎呢。” 嘉莱缪再次紧紧拥抱了她的儿子。 　　 出版商说明： 　　 我过往不情愿出版马洛巴尔·苏的著作，但当格维林大学出版社请我编辑该版时，我决定乘此机会一劳永逸地直接宣明。 学者们对马洛巴尔·苏完成著作的准确年代尚存争议，但已知它们均为剧作家“歌耳·费琳”所作，他在第一希罗帝尔帝国倒台到泰伯·塞普汀崛起之间的空位时期因创作流行喜剧和浪漫故事闻名。今天一种理论称，费琳把某些他听过的锻莫真实故事改动重编成他自己的剧本，随后搬上舞台大赚一笔。 歌耳·费琳虚构了“马洛巴尔·苏”这个可以翻译锻莫语的角色，以求给其著作增加些许可信度，也让它们对于那些容易受骗的人们而言更有价值。不过注意一点：在“马洛巴尔·苏”及其著作成为热烈争议的中心话题时，从无某人确切见过“马洛巴尔·苏”本人的可信记录，也没有同名者受雇于法师公会、尤里安诺斯学派或其他任何学术机构。 　　 不管怎样，“马洛巴尔·苏”所作故事中绝大多数锻莫都与那个令人生畏、深不可测，甚至能让丹莫、诺德人和红卫人吓得屈服，并建造了至今仍不为人所解的众多遗迹的种族，几乎没有相似之处。

eavy armor must be designed to take a lot of punishment. It will receive direct blows from all sorts of weapons while protecting the wearer. Interviews With Tapestrists Volume Eighteen Cherim's Heart of Anequina by Livillus Perus, Professor at the Imperial University

[pagebreak] [pagebreak]

ontemporary with Maqamat Lusign (interviewed in volume seventeen of this series) is the Khajiti Cherim, whose tapestries have been hailed as masterpieces all over the Empire for nigh on thirty years now. His four factories located throughout Elsweyr make reproductions of his work, but his original tapestries command stellar prices. The Emperor himself owns ten Cherim tapestries, and his representatives are currently negotiating the sale of five more. The muted use of color contrasted with the luminous skin tones of Cherim's subjects is a marked contrast with the old style of tapestry. The subjects of his work in recent years have been fabulous tales of the ancient past: the Gods meeting to discuss the formation of the world; the Chimer following the Prophet Veloth into Morrowind; the Wild Elves battling Morihaus and his legions at the White Gold Tower. His earliest designs dealt with more contemporary subjects. I had the opportunity to discuss with him one of his first masterpieces, The Heart of Anequina, at his villa in Orcrest. The Heart of Anequina presents an historic battle of the Five Year War between Elsweyr and Valenwood which raged from 3E 394 (or 3E 395, depending on what one considers to be the beginning of the war) until 3E 399. In most fair accounts, the war lasted 4 years and 9 months, but artistic license from the great epic poets added an additional three months to the ordeal. The actual details of the battle itself, as interpreted by Cherim, are explicit. The faces of a hundred and twenty Wood Elf archers can be differentiated one from the other, each registering fear at the approach of the Khajiti army. Their hauberks catch the dim light of the sun. The menacing shadows of the Elsweyr battlecats loom on the hills, every muscle strained, ready to pounce in command. It is not surprising that he got all the details right, because Cherim was in the midst of it, as a Khajiti foot soldier. Every minute part of the Khajiti traditional armor can be seen in the soldiers in the foreground. The embroidered edging and striped patterns on the tunics. Each lacquered plate on loose-fitting leather in the Elsweyr style. The helmets of cloth and fluted silver. "Cherim does not understand the point of plate mail," said Cherim. "It is hot, for one, like being both burned and buried alive. Cherim wore it at the insistence of our Nord advisors during the Battle of Zelinin, and Cherim couldn't even turn to see what my fellow Khajiit were doing. Cherim did some sketches for a tapestry of the Battle of Zelinin, but Cherim finds that to make it realistic, the figures came out very mechanical, like iron golems or dwemer centurions. Knowing our Khajiti commanders, Cherim would not be surprised if giving up the heavy plate was more aesthetic than practical." "Elsweyr lost the Battle of Zelinin, didn't she?" "Yes, but Elsweyr won the war, starting at the next battle, the Heart of Anequina," said Cherim with a smile. "The tide turned as soon as we Khajiit sent our Nordic advisors back to Solitude. We had to get rid of all the heavy armor they brought to us and find enough traditional armor our troops felt comfortable wearing. Obviously, the principle advantage of the traditional armor was that we could move easily in it, as you can see from the natural stances of the soldiers in the tapestry. "Now if you look at this poor perforated Cathay-raht who just keeps battling on in the bottom background, you see the other advantage. It seems strange to say, but one of the best features of traditional armor is that an arrow will either deflect completely or pass all the way through. An arrow head is like a hook, made to stick where it strikes if it doesn't pass through. A soldier in traditional armor will find himself with a hole in his body and the bolt on the other side. Our healers can fix such a wound easily if it isn't fatal, but if the arrow still remains in the armor, as it does with heavier armor, the wound will be reopened every time the fellow moves. Unless the Khajiit strips off the armor and pulls out the arrow, which is what we had to do at the Battle of Zelinin. A difficult and time-consuming process in the heat of battle, to say the least." I asked him next, "Is there a self portrait in the battle?" "Yes," Cherim said with another grin. "You see the small figure of the Khajiit stealing the rings off the dead Wood Elf? His back is facing you, but he has a brown and orange striped tail like Cherim's. Cherim does not say that all stereotypes about the Khajiit are fair, but Cherim must sometimes acknowledge them." A self-deprecating style in self-portraiture is also evident in the tapestries of Ranulf Hook, the next artist interviewed in volume nineteen of this series.

与玛卡马特·卢塞恩（在本系列第17卷访谈）同时代的卡吉特切瑞姆，他的织锦杰作享誉于帝国各地已近三十年。他在艾斯维尔的四家工厂都在复制他的作品，但他的织锦原作却要价不菲。像皇帝本人已拥有十件切瑞姆织锦，但他的代表们目前正在洽谈添置另外五件或更多的事宜。 运用的暗淡色彩与切瑞姆主题的鲜亮肤色相对照着，与以往织锦的风格形成鲜明对比。近些年来，他的作品都以过往的远古传奇故事为主题：众神开会讨论世界的构造、凯莫跟随先知维洛斯进入晨风、野精灵在白金塔与莫里豪斯及其军团作战。不过他的早期设计则涉及更当代的主题。在他位于或峰的别墅中，我有幸与他就其最早杰作之一--《安内奎那之心》展开了一番讨论。 艾斯维尔与威伦森林之间曾经历过从第三纪元394年（或395年，这取决于个人认为战争的开始是什么）到399年的“五年战争”，在大多数公正的记载中，这场战争持续了四年零九个月，但来自伟大咏史诗人的艺术加工给这场磨难增加了三个月时间。《安内奎那之心》正是展示其中一场历史性的战役。 切瑞姆将战争的细节演绎的淋漓尽致。你可以辨别出这一百二十个木精灵射手面孔上的不同，同时每个都表现出对卡吉特军队到来的恐惧。然后他们的锁子甲也都反射着微弱的阳光。而来势汹汹的艾斯维尔战争之猫的影子笼罩丘陵上，他们绷紧了每块肌肉，随时准备在命令下突袭。不过切瑞姆能把所有细节都说对了也没有什么可惊讶的，毕竟他当时正作为一名卡吉特步兵处于这场战役中。 在前景的士兵身上可以看到卡吉特传统护甲的每块小零件——束腰外衣上的刺绣饰边与条纹图案、艾斯维尔风格的宽松皮革上的每块漆甲、布盔上镶着的银纹。 “切瑞姆不明白板甲有什么用，”切瑞姆说，“穿着板甲会很闷，就像要被埋起来活活烧死一样。在泽利宁战役中，切瑞姆在我们诺德顾问们的坚持下穿上了它，然后切瑞姆甚至不能回头看看我的卡吉特同伴在做什么。切瑞姆曾为关于泽利宁战役的织锦做了一些草图，但切瑞姆发现如果要真实再现它，会让人物表现得非常机械，就像铁魔像或是锻莫百夫长一样。对于了解我们的卡吉特指挥官，如果他们选择放弃那些美观远胜实用的重板，切瑞姆也不会感到惊讶。” “艾斯维尔输掉了泽利宁战役，不是么？” “是的，但从下一场战役——安内奎那之心开始，艾斯维尔最终还是赢得了这场战争，”切瑞姆笑着说，“当我们卡吉特将我们的诺德顾问们送回独孤后，形势就发生变化了。我们必须处理掉他们带来的所有重型护甲，然后找来足够多的让我们觉得佩戴舒适的传统护甲。很明显，传统护甲的根本优势就在于我们可以自如移动，就像你可以从织锦上士兵的自然状态中看到的一样。” “如果现在你看看这个只是在背景底部继续战斗、被射穿的可怜卡塞-拉特，你会看到传统护甲的另一个优势。说起来可能很奇怪，但这就是传统护甲的最强特色之一——射中的箭矢要么被完全偏斜掉，要么就彻底贯穿身体。箭头就像是钩子，如果不穿过去就会牢牢地扎在击中的地方。而穿着传统护甲的士兵则只会发现身上有个洞和在边上的箭矢。如果这一箭并不致命，我们的治疗师就可以很轻易地修复这样的伤口；但如果像重型护甲那样箭还留在护甲里的话，伤口会在他每次移动时重新撕开。除非卡吉特脱掉护甲拔出箭来，在泽利宁战役中我们就不得不这么做了。不夸张地说，在进入白热化的战役中，这是个艰难而耗时的操作。” 我又问他：“你有把战役中的自己画上去么？” “当然，”切瑞姆又笑着说，“你看到那个小小的卡吉特人物了吗？在扒那死木精灵的戒指、背对着你、有着和切瑞姆一样棕橙条纹尾巴的那个。切瑞姆并没有说所有对卡吉特的刻板印象都是公正的，但切瑞姆有时候必须承认它们。” 这种以自画像的形式来自嘲的风格在兰多夫·胡克的织锦中也很明显，他也是接下来本系列第19卷要采访的艺术家。

Light Armor Forging By Revus Sarvani
